articles.title: As Abbott Elementary Fans Hope For Janine And Gregory’s Engagement At Disneyland, I Have A Question
articles.summary: Let's talk about another Abbott couple?
articles.content:
For six seasons now, Abbott Elementary fans have faithfully watched the relationship between Janine Teagues (Quinta Brunson) and Gregory Eddie (Tyler James Williams) progress. The pair have gone from good friends to committed lovers over the past several years and, now, it seems we’re on the cusp of a proposal. Many viewers are hoping an engagement will come during the Disneyland-set 100th episode that’ll air amid the 2026 TV schedule . I’d love that as well, but I also have a question about two other characters.

Gregory and Janine are, of course, the core couple on Abbott , but plenty of other romantic relationships amongst characters have been highlighted as well. As we anticipate what lies ahead for Janine and Gregory, I can’t help but wonder what the future holds for Ava Coleman and O’Shon, who’ve been dating since Season 4. I’ve enjoyed seeing their relationship develop as well as the funny moments that have resulted from that. With that, it’s hard not to wonder what the long-term plan for them might look like.

Gregory first expressed interest in proposing to Janine at the end of Season 5, which was about two years after the two finally got together. Ava and O’Shon will be reaching that mark later in the sixth season and, while great TV couples have different timelines, I could see O’Shon popping the question soon. Plus, given how encouraging O’Shon has been amid Gregory’s attempts to propose, who’s to say the former doesn’t want that for himself sometime in the near future?

Of course, I’m not saying anyone needs to be jumping the broom by the end of this season. I just wouldn’t mind seeing one or two engagements by the time Abbott’s finale rolls around next spring. That may seem like a long shot for Ava and O’Shon right now, but I’m feeling very good about Janine and Gregory’s chances of hitting that milestone.

Gregory has been trying to orchestrate the right moment to present Janine with a ring. During the show’s latest episode, “Competition,” he attempted to land a reservation at a popular Italian restaurant, where he could propose. Ironically, that plan became moot once Abbott’s Step Team punched their ticket to Disneyland, and Janine informed her man that they’d serve as chaperones on the trip. So it now seems like a given that Gregory will attempt to propose while he and his lady are in “The Happiest Place On Earth.”

articles.title: Steven Spielberg's Western Officially Revealed, And 4 Other Oscar Winners Are Confirmed Too
articles.summary: After returning to science fiction with this year’s critically acclaimed Disclosure Day, Oscar-winning director Steven Spielberg’s next film will be his first Western. The legendary filmmaker is set to helm The Heart in Winter, an adaptation of the 2024 novel of the same name by Kevin Barry, and Spielberg is not the only big name […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google After returning to science fiction with this year’s critically acclaimed Disclosure Day , Oscar-winning director Steven Spielberg ’s next film will be his first Western. The legendary filmmaker is set to helm The Heart in Winter , an adaptation of the 2024 novel of the same name by Kevin Barry, and Spielberg is not the only big name attached to the Universal and Focus Features project. Paul Thomas Anderson, whose previous film One Battle After Another is the most recent winner of the Academy Award for Best Picture, is set to write The Heart in Winter ’s screenplay. In addition, Cillian Murphy, Jessie Buckley, and Mark Rylance, all of whom have themselves won Oscars, have been cast in principal roles.

Like the novel, The Heart in Winter is described as focusing on a pair of star-crossed lovers living in the American West, who will be played by Buckley and Murphy. Buckley won the Best Actress category at this year’s Oscars for her performance in Hamnet , which Spielberg was a producer on, while Murphy took home the Best Actor prize for his work in the leading role of Christopher Nolan’s 2023 biopic Oppenheimer . Rylance won Best Supporting Actor for his portrayal of a real life convicted spy in the 2015 historical drama Bridge of Spies , which Spielberg also directed.

Spielberg and Anderson have personally won three Oscars each, with many other films they’ve contributed to having received other awards and nominations. Spielberg has won Best Director twice, for 1993’s Schindler’s List and 1998’s Saving Private Ryan , the former of which also won Best Picture. Spielberg has frequently spoken of his admiration for many Western films and the influence the genre has had on his work, which is made apparent by references and homages in many of his projects, including the semi-autobiographical film The Fabelmans , which contains a fictionalized depiction of Spielberg’s own first meeting with director John Ford, played in the 2022 film by David Lynch.

In addition to finally venturing into the Western genre directly, Spielberg has emphasized that the prospect of working with Anderson, a close friend of his, influenced his decision to direct The Heart in Winter . The film is the first narrative feature Anderson has written for another filmmaker to direct, suggesting that he was similarly enthusiastic about working with Spielberg. Anderson also won the Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay for One Battle After Another . The Heart in Winter is currently set for release on an unspecified date in 2028.

Are you excited for Spielberg's first Western? Discuss in the comments.

articles.title: 4 DC Cartoons That Deserve a A Reboot, Including a Forgotten Batman Series
articles.summary: While DC has had and continues to have a tumultuous history in live-action, the franchise has consistently thrived in animation. Throughout its history, there have been some amazing animated series, from Batman: The Animated Series (1992) and The Batman (2004) to Caped Crusader (2024) and Justice League Unlimited (2004). While most ended on their terms, […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google While DC has had and continues to have a tumultuous history in live-action , the franchise has consistently thrived in animation. Throughout its history, there have been some amazing animated series, from Batman: The Animated Series (1992) and The Batman (2004) to Caped Crusader (2024) and Justice League Unlimited (2004). While most ended on their terms, some ended sooner than they deserved, whether through cancellation or being left in limbo.

These four DC cartoons are among those great series and definitely deserve to make a comeback. And while some of these series might be familiar, there's one one forgotten Batman series we can't help but mention.

One of the most beloved DC Comics animated shows to date, Teen Titans premiered in 2003 and ran until 2006. The series followed the titular superhero team, comprised of Robin (Scott Menville), Raven (Tara Strong), Cyborg (Khary Payton), Starfire (Hynden Walch), and Beast Boy (Greg Cipes). Led by Robin (Batman’s sidekick), the Teen Titans protected the West Coast metropolis of Jump City from crime, often of the supervillainous variety. Throughout the series, the teens would also experience the struggles that go along with adolescence. The series ran for five seasons totaling 65 episodes, plus the film Teen Titans: Trouble in Tokyo , which served as the series finale. Each season had a different overarching villain, often connected to a member of the team, such as Trigon (Kevin Michael Richardson) in season five, the evil father of Raven.

The exact reason Teen Titans came to an end remains unknown. Will Wheaton claimed that Warner Bros. executives didn't like the pitch for the sixth season. Story editor Rob Hoegee said it was Cartoon Network's decision and that it was known ahead of time that the series was ending. Two more explanations were proposed by writer and producer David Stack. He said it could have been because of toy licensing (Mattel had all Cartoon Network licenses but not the Teen Titans license) or a drop in ratings during the fifth season as a result of their darker fourth season. Whatever the reason, the series was fantastic and remains a beloved part of DC animation history. Fans and the series cast continue to push for a sixth season return, and one would be well deserved.

Green Lantern: The Animated Series aired on Cartoon Network from March 2012 to March 2013, following a one-hour preview in November 2011. The series followed Green Lanterns Hal Jordan (Josh Keaton) and Kilowog (Kevin Michael Richardson), Red Lantern-turned-Blue Lantern Razer (Jason Spisak), and Green Lantern artificial intelligence Aya (Grey DeLisle) as they fought the Red Lanterns and Manhunters (a very different kind from the one seen in Lanterns ). It was the first Green Lantern series, the first DC series animated completely in CGI, and the first CGI series to be developed by Bruce Timm. The series tapped deeply into the lore. It featured the origins of Mogo, the planet that becomes a Green Lantern, and introduced other colors of ring-bearers.

Despite positive audience reception and viewership, the series ran for just one season of 26 episodes before being cancelled by Cartoon Network. This was in response to the low sales of the toys released for the show, which were impacted by the 2011 Green Lantern movie. The two projects were released in close proximity to one another, causing toys for the film to still be in stores, and the poor performance and negative reviews for it caused the audience to not buy them. Then, when the toys for the series came out, they didn't sell well either, and some stores didn't even carry them because of the full stock that remained for the film merchandise. The fallout from the film hurt the series and led to its premature cancellation. The series maintains a strong fanbase to this day, however, with viewers thrilled when it was put up to watch for free on Tubi after multiple years without it streaming. If any DC animated series deserves a comeback, it is Green Lantern: The Animated Series .

One of the most forgotten Batman series, Beware the Batman aired for one season and 26 episodes, just like Green Lantern: The Animated Series . The series followed Bruce Wayne (Anthony Ruivivar) in his early years as Gotham's masked protector. Together with his former MI6 butler Alfred Pennyworth (JB Blanc), bodyguard/partner Tatsu Yamashiro/Katana (Sumalee Montano), and eventually Lt. James Gordon (Kurtwood Smith), he protected Gotham from his Rogues Gallery. The series was unable to utilize most of Batman's most iconic villains, so it had to rely on his less commonly used ones. It did so to great success, featuring fantastic versions of characters like Professor Pyg, Humpty Dumpty, and Anarky (who became the series' main antagonist). But it was able to use classic Rogues as well, like Killer Croc, Ra's Al Ghul, and an interesting new take on Deathstroke.

The series had a rough time on television, which hurt its viewership. It premiered in July 2013, but was pulled from the air just three months later without an explanation. In May, the series moved to Cartoon Network's Toonami block, airing in the early morning. The terrible scheduling caused Beware the Batman to have low viewership. The network called the series a financial failure and canceled it. The final seven episodes were aired as a marathon on September 28th, allowing the series to end properly, though on a cliffhanger that remains unresolved a decade later. While its CGI animation was on the bland side, the story and performances were fantastic. The series deserves a continuation and a proper resolution to its story.

1.) Young Justice (2010-2022) Young Justice began as a series focused on classic Justice League hero sidekicks Robin (Jesse McCartney), Kid Flash (Jason Spisak), and Aqualad (Khary Payton) as they teamed up with new heroes Superboy (Nolan North), Miss Martian (Danica McKellar), and Artemis (Stephanie Lemalin) as they formed a new covert team within the League. The series would change a lot over time, growing with the core cast and introducing many new young heroes into the mix. It started as a teen drama, but eventually evolved into a mature adult drama that could get pretty dark at times (especially in one particular episode of season four). The series was also canon-adjacent to Green Lantern: The Animated Series , and Razer (once again voiced by Jason Spisak) appeared and continued his story from the series.

Like Beware the Batman , Young Justice also had a difficult production history. The series ran for four seasons, totaling 98 episodes. The first two seasons aired on Cartoon Network from 2010 to 2013 before being cancelled due to low toy sales cutting funding from Mattel. There was strong fan support for the series, which ultimately resulted in a renewal for a third season in 2016 that was released in 2019 on the now-defunct DC Universe service. A fourth season was greenlit later that same year and was released on HBO Max from late 2021 to June 2022. Since then, the series has sat in limbo. It has never been cancelled or renewed. The fanbase for the series remains passionate and continues to campaign for its revival. James Gunn said his plans for the DCU were inspired by Young Justice and Justice League Unlimited , renewing hopes that the series could return. With his controversial departure as DC Studios co-CEO, the future of the series is even more uncertain. Young Justice was a fantastic series that ended on a cliffhanger, and it deserves to continue.

What DC animated series do you wish would return? Let us know down in the comments.

articles.title: PS1 Exclusive Game Stealth Released on PS5 and Switch 2 After 31 Years
articles.summary: A PS1 exclusive game from 1995 has been stealth-released on PS5 and Nintendo Switch 2 after 31 years. This is the game's first re-release and marks the first time it has ever been available on a Nintendo platform. To this end, Nintendo fans may have no familiarity with the new release, but they may know […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google A PS1 exclusive game from 1995 has been stealth-released on PS5 and Nintendo Switch 2 after 31 years. This is the game's first re-release and marks the first time it has ever been available on a Nintendo platform. To this end, Nintendo fans may have no familiarity with the new release, but they may know the game's predecessor, which was notably an SNES exclusive. To go from a Nintendo exclusive to a PlayStation exclusive with a sequel is incredibly rare.

The new re-release comes from Japanese developer Hamster Corporation, which specializes in re-releasing niche games from yesteryear, often plucked from the catalogs of the NES, SNES, and PS1. Its latest re-release is The Firemen 2: Pete & Danny from developer Media Entertainment and publisher Human Entertainment, neither of which exists anymore. What makes this particular release even more particular is that it not only took the series from Nintendo to PlayStation exclusivity, but that the first game got a Western release, while the sequel did not. To this end, this is also the first time the game has been available outside of Japan.

Unfortunately, while the game has been released in the West, and is no longer trapped to a PS1 disc impossible to find, it has not been localized. It's not text- or dialogue-heavy, but you won't be getting the full experience if you don't know Japanese, and you may struggle to play it at all. Meanwhile, as you can see from the trailer below, the game doesn't quite hold up in 2026. If you don't have nostalgia for it or the first game, it's probably not going to be a worthwhile time travel back to 1995. Those who are interested, though, will find it available for $11.99. The eShop does not have user reviews, but the PS Store does, and on there, so far, it has a perfect score.

A 32-Bit PS1 Game From Yesteryear For those just learning about The Firemen 2, it is an action-adventure game where you play as Pete and Danny, two members of the New York City District D Fire Station, First Platoon, who must save people trapped in a burning super-tall amusement building.

That said, it's worth noting this isn't the original in its purest form. It is the original game, but some modern features are available to modern players. More precisely, customizable button layouts, rapid-fire settings, multiple save points, rewind functionality, adjustable screen layout options, and CRT filters have all been added with the port.

If this PS1 nostalgia does not tickle your fancy, or if you're on a tighter budget, a remaster of an entire PS1 trilogy is currently available for just $2.54 , which is less than $1 per game included.

articles.title: New Xbox Report Claims the Brand Has Considered Ditching One of Its Most Divisive Features With Project Helix
articles.summary: A new report tied to Xbox has claimed that the brand nearly chose to abandon one of its most divisive features with its upcoming Project Helix hardware. While the Xbox 360 is by far the most popular Xbox console in history, it also introduced something that many users are still frustrated by: paid multiplayer. Rather […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google A new report tied to Xbox has claimed that the brand nearly chose to abandon one of its most divisive features with its upcoming Project Helix hardware . While the Xbox 360 is by far the most popular Xbox console in history, it also introduced something that many users are still frustrated by: paid multiplayer. Rather than being able to play any online multiplayer title for free on Xbox consoles, users have to pay to subscribe to Xbox Game Pass, or what was previously Xbox Live Gold . And while paid subscriptions for multiplayer are still required on Xbox and PlayStation platforms alike, Xbox leadership is said to have considered finally doing away with it, but may have now reversed course.

According to Windows Central , previous Xbox leadership intended to finally get away from the need to subscribe to a membership in order to play multiplayer titles on Xbox hardware with Project Helix. This plan was said to be rooted in the fact that Project Helix is meant to blur the lines between Xbox consoles and PCs, as it will instead be a hybrid of the two. With PCs not requiring a need to subscribe to any sort of service to play multiplayer games, Xbox seemed to think that continuing to do so on Project Helix wouldn't make much sense. However, the report claims that this plan might no longer be the case.

Following the retirement of Phil Spencer earlier this year , newly appointed Xbox boss Asha Sharma is said to have overhauled some long-term strategies for the company. One such change is related to Project Helix, which is said to now be more of a console-first platform that can also play PC games rather than the inverse, which is reportedly how it was conceived at first. Because Project Helix is now going to be more in line with how past Xbox consoles were, it's reportedly much less likely that Microsoft would drop the need for paid subscriptions when it comes to multiplayer games.

On one hand, it's easy to see why Xbox wouldn't want to do away with this need for paywalled multiplayer, as it's a simple way for the company to continue generating revenue. On the other hand, if Xbox were to scrap such a requirement, it would give it a distinct leg up against PlayStation, which is its most direct competition. No matter what Xbox leadership ultimately decides, it will surely still have an uphill battle when it comes to selling Project Helix, as the next-gen platform is reportedly on track to cost as much as $2,000 whenever it does arrive .

What do you think about this potential for Xbox to finally make multiplayer games free for everyone? And if it doesn't do away with paywalled multiplayer, will you be upset? Be sure to let me know down in the comments section.

articles.title: Everyone Knows Ted Kord and Jaime Reyes, but the Original Blue Beetle Was a Whole Different Kind of Hero
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics The Blue Beetle is one of DC's most enduring legacies, with Jaime Reyes being the most popular and the previous Beetle, Ted Kord, standing as one of DC's most shocking deaths. Both of these heroes have made a serious name for themselves, and both helped make the Blue Beetle name something every DC fan has […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The Blue Beetle is one of DC's most enduring legacies, with Jaime Reyes being the most popular and the previous Beetle, Ted Kord, standing as one of DC's most shocking deaths. Both of these heroes have made a serious name for themselves, and both helped make the Blue Beetle name something every DC fan has heard of. Sure, Blue Beetle isn't a household name like Batman or Wonder Woman, but he stands at the cusp of superhero stardom. Heck, he even starred in his own solo movie, which is as sure a sign that a hero has made it as any other.

However, Ted and Jaime aren't the only ones who've called themselves the Blue Beetle. In fact, there was actually a third hero who took up the name, creating the identity that both would go on to make famous. Daniel Garrett was the original Blue Beetle, and his origins are actually incredibly important to the modern interpretations of the hero, but he's also so much more. He's actually the missing link that connects the Blue Beetle to every facet of power in DC, and living proof that a good reinvention could be all a hero needs to break into the spotlight.

The original Blue Beetle was actually Dan Garret, appearing in the Fox Feature Syndicate. He was a normal man who was granted incredible strength and durability by a neighborhood pharmacist's special drug, Vitamin 2-X. Donning Dr. Franz's blue, bullet-proof chainmail, he became one of the earliest Mystery Men. This version was a typical fighting man for the period, even having a sidekick named Sparky, who was a clear Buck rip-off. There's not much interesting about this version of the character, but things really took a unique turn when the Blue Beetle was reimagined as Dan Garrett, with two Ts, for the Silver Age by Charlton Comics.

This Dan was an archeologist who uncovered a mystical blue scarab while working in Egypt. It granted him incredible abilities, such as increased strength and flight, and even provided his Blue Beetle costume. Eventually, he was killed in action fighting his roommate Ted Kord's evil uncle and his robot army. Dan passed his Scarab and mission of justice onto Ted, but the new Beetle found that the Scarab refused to work for him, and had to make do with his own physique and advanced technology. Dan's origin would be slightly tweaked again when DC finally acquired the rights to his character , with him instead being Ted's college professor and leaving a family who knew his secret identity.

However, that wasn't the end of Charlton's work with the Blue Beetle. The team working on him actually planned to restore Dan, revealing that both Garret and Garrett were actually the same man, a chosen warrior of unknown gods. He would constantly reincarnate in new lives set up for him to act as their vessel, fighting crime as an immortal warrior across the ages. The company would never be able to pursue this storyline, but it was published in Americomics #3, which gave us this look at this first attempt to consolidate the Blue Beetle's various origins. Although this is the only time it would be done exclusively for Dan, it was far from the last rework for the Blue Beetle.

The Blue Beetle, more than any other heroic legacy, shows just how effective a change in direction can be for capturing the audience's attention. The original was a drop in the bucket of similar heroes, with nothing to set him apart from the multitudes of other heroes who did the exact same things he did. First, he utilized experimental drugs, but later he would shift hard into the mystical angle. Ted was a step in a completely different direction, using high tech and no superpowers, aiming for more of a Batman-inspired role while still bringing his own style. Jaime, meanwhile, uses the Scarab, but its history was reworked to be alien in origin, giving him a high-tech battlesuit that could create any weapon he could imagine.

From drugs to magic to science to alien technology, the Blue Beetle has changed drastically with each incarnation, and it's inspiring. Creators have been trying to make the character work for generations, each team passing the torch to the next as they refined what worked and left behind what didn't. Ted captured far more of an audience than Dan, but when he became stale and was killed in dramatic fashion, Jaime emerged with his own distinct style that elevated the hero even more. Blue Beetle is a perfect showcase of DC's incredible dedication to heroic legacies , as the company is willing to do just about anything to make the hero work.

Blue Beetle has origins that touch on just about every source of origins in DC, and each one provided a unique take on a hero that kept growing more and more with every year. Each incarnation is radically different from the last, to the point where you'd think their only similarities are their names, but each pays so much homage to what came before. Every Blue Beetle has been instrumental in the character's growth, and every person who dons the blue understands and respects that. More than anyone else, the Blue Beetle is a hero who honors the past even as he forges his own path, and that is the perfect style for any legacy hero.

Which Blue Beetle is your favorite? I love Ted and Booster, but my heart definitely belongs to Jaime. Let us know your number one Beetle in the comments below!

Avatar: Seven Havens is a sort of clean break […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Avatar: Seven Havens has a much different look to it than fans saw with the previous Avatar: The Last Airbender outings, and one of the producers behind it all has addressed why the series has been changed so much with its art style and animation techniques. Avatar: Seven Havens is a sort of clean break from the rest of the franchise as it takes place hundreds of years after the events of The Legend of Korra . And that comes with a drastic change in the way it's designed its world too.

Avatar: Seven Havens executive producer Ethan Spaulding recently took part in a Reddit AMA for the series, and had been asked by fans why it looks so different than from what was seen in the prior series with characters having larger eyes and different proportions. As Spaulding explained, this was due to Avatar: Seven Havens being imagined with a "more obvious anime style " as the team was going for a more fantasy based look for its world.

"With all of the Avatar properties there is always a change in look and style , Seven Havens was always imagined as having a more obvious anime style to its characters," Spaulding explained. "We were going for a more fantasy based look and it being a Post Cataclysmic world this aesthetic choice seemed a good fit." When it comes to the actual animation of the series, Spaulding noted that the team wanted to lean into the "limited" style seen in other anime releases with plans to save it for the bigger moments.

"The decision was to lean into ‘limited animation’ as anime does and have fuller animation when the scenes really called for it, and yes time and budget is always a consideration in a tv series," Spaulding revealed. For those fans questioning the series' fluidity, Spaulding also stated, "The animation keeps getting better and better as the series progresses." That has already been seen with episodes like the first season's final few, and that's likely going to be case with the bigger episodes coming in the future.

"The Bigger tentpole finale episodes do get a bigger budget and also it is natural as a new series progresses," Spaulding also revealed when asked if the bigger episodes do get a more sizable budget. The producer also noted that "the animation gets better and better as animators become more familiar with animating the designs." Avatar: Seven Havens has been in the works for the last few years, so it's likely that the series is going to get even bigger and better from here as Pavi heads into the other Havens .

One of the drawbacks of this first Avatar: Seven Havens was the lack of one on one fights compared to what was seen in other series, but that's likely going to change now that the other Havens are set to be revealed. Avatar: Seven Havens Season 2 is going to be hitting Paramount+ next May, with Season 3 hitting in late 2027. The series will then come to an end with Season 4 , so there's all sorts of opportunity for big moments. But how are you feeling about Avatar: Seven Havens ' art style and animation so far? Let us know your thoughts about it in the comments.

articles.title: Disneyland’s Fantasmic Once Again Went Up In Flames, And I’m Starting To Worry About The Show’s Future
articles.summary: This is not a good sign!
articles.content:
Disneyland live entertainment is few and far between as of late, which is a shame considering the Anaheim theme park used to boast some of the best shows. On November 21st, one of the last and most beloved nighttime shows, Fantasmic, went up in flames for the second time in three short years. With two incidents and Disney’s desire to cut back on live entertainment, I’m really starting to worry about the future of the show.

The fire reportedly broke out during Fantasmic’s second performance of the night shortly before the show’s finale. While the Mark Twain finale was able to go on, flames can be seen behind the boat on the small stage set up on Tom Saywer Island. Guests at the park were quick to pull out their phones and film the growing flames as the Mark Twain, full of classic Disney characters , made its way around the river. Take a look:

The last two minutes of the show were canceled, and guests were asked to vacate the viewing area while the fire department handled the blaze. Thankfully, the fire was small compared to the 2023 incident that turned the Maleficent dragon animatronic into a giant fireball and forever changed the show. There’s been no word on the extent of the damage this time around, but considering the show was back Sunday night it safe to assume that nothing was affected and no cast members were harmed, thankfully.

Two fiery incidents are definitely a cause for concern, and with Disneyland executives’ history of scaling back entertainment to cut costs, I can’t help but worry about the show’s fate. After all, Fantasmic boasts a large cast of incredible performers and several floating units. Plus water screens, projectors, and fireworks. I’m no expert, but I’m willing to bet it’s one of the most costly attractions at Disneyland. Not to mention, the show is still feeling the loss of the Maleficent Dragon, which makes the battle between Mickey and Maleficent lackluster.

articles.title: GTA 6 Is a Reminder That Open-World Games Should Give Players More Freedom to Complete Missions
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Rockstar Games There's a contradiction at the heart of many open-world games where developers spend years building enormous environments for players to explore anyway they please, only to suddenly become very particular about what they're allowed to do once a mission begins. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google There's a contradiction at the heart of many open-world games where developers spend years building enormous environments for players to explore anyway they please, only to suddenly become very particular about what they're allowed to do once a mission begins. Take a different route? Mission failed. Try an unexpected approach? Mission failed. Use a perfectly reasonable tool that the game has used hours teaching you to use? Somehow, also mission failed. It's a frustrating disconnect, particularly when the whole appeal of an open-world game is supposed to be the freedom to make your own decisions.

For this reason, among others, Rockstar has spent a long time refining its approach to mission design. Grand Theft Auto IV is an encouraging step toward resolving that contradiction. The studio has made a conscious effort to accommodate different approaches instead of constantly pulling players back toward one prescribed solution. Allowing for player agency is one of the most powerful tools a developer has, and it's something the entire industry could stand to embrace more often.

Rockstar's approach to mission design has been controversial on the small scale for quite a long time now. Their open worlds encourage players to experiment with practically everything, but that freedom can disappear the moment a story mission begins. GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 are particularly familiar examples of this disconnect, with missions that often expect players to follow a very specific sequence of events. You might have an entire arsenal at your disposal, yet suddenly find yourself unable to use a particular weapon because the mission expects something else. Even wandering too far from the intended route can bring an abrupt end to an otherwise successful attempt. There's a difference between guiding players toward an objective and insisting they complete every step exactly as the developers imagined.

GTA 6 makes a welcome effort to loosen those restrictions, and that becomes apparent within the first few hours. Missions feel less concerned with keeping players on a predetermined path, giving them more room to improvise when things don't go according to plan. Whether you're approaching an objective from an unexpected direction or finding your own way out of a dangerous situation, the game is more willing to accommodate decisions that might once have resulted in an immediate mission failure. It doesn't mean every situation has countless possible solutions, but there's a greater sense that players are allowed to figure things out for themselves. That's a meaningful shift in how Rockstar approaches the relationship between its authored missions and the people playing them.

I particularly appreciate that this doesn't require Rockstar to abandon what makes its storytelling work. There are moments when a mission needs to deliver a specific sequence of events, and giving players complete control over every interaction would make that considerably harder to accomplish. There's a considerable amount of space between a completely scripted sequence and an experience with no creative direction. GTA 6 demonstrates that developers can preserve the moments they want players to experience without dictating every single step required to reach them.

The games that stick with us most are the ones that give us something to talk about afterward because of something we did, not something obviously pre-ordained. Maybe a carefully planned encounter went completely sideways, or an unexpected decision created a situation the developers somehow anticipated. Those moments can be far more memorable than a perfectly choreographed sequence because they belong to the player. When you are responsible for that insane sequence of events that somehow let to a success, that distinction makes an enormous difference in how we remember an experience.

This why player agency should always be an absolute priority for developers across practically every genre, even those built around relatively linear narratives. A tightly authored adventure doesn't need branching storylines or dozens of different endings to give players meaningful control. Sometimes it's enough to let someone approach a combat encounter with their preferred strategy instead of insisting they use a particular ability. Other times, it means allowing players to interact with an environment in ways that feel natural rather than arbitrarily restricting them because the designers only accounted for one solution. Those decisions might seem relatively minor during development, but they can completely change how someone experiences a game. More importantly, they give players ownership over the moments they're creating.

There's a reason people love sharing stories about the ridiculous things that happened during their playthroughs. Those experiences become personal in a way that a developer's carefully constructed set piece rarely can, even when that set piece is spectacular. I don't want every game to become an immersive sim, nor do I think developers should sacrifice their creative vision in pursuit of endless possibilities. But there's a difference between giving players a story to experience and giving them the tools to make that experience their own. GTA 6 is a strong step in the right direction, that those two things don't have to work against each other. I'd love to see more developers recognize just how much that freedom can add to their games.

Do you prefer open-ended missions that let you experiment, or more tightly scripted experiences designed around a specific vision? Feel free to scribe your thoughts in the comments below.

articles.title: How Becoming A Mom Is Already Affecting Hailee Steinfeld Picking New Movie Roles
articles.summary: Here's what the Hawkeye actress is doing "moving forward".
articles.content:
Hailee Steinfeld just became a mama earlier this year when her and her husband Josh Allen welcomed their daughter in the spring . It was just confirmed that she’s got not one but two projects among upcoming 2026 movies – now that the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer showed Kate Bishop among the massive roster of heroes. But will her new starring role in her daughter’s life change how she approaches Hollywood going forward?

The beginning of Steinfeld’s answer reminds me how she famously decided to explore her own mixed heritage roots when she got to play Mary in Sinners . The actress said that the research for that role was looking into her family history, and that brought her closer to her mother and her grandfather, who account for the Filipino and African American side of her ancestry. These days she’s going to also think of her daughter too when she picks jobs, too. As Steinfeld said herself:

Steinfeld’s latest movie is Walt Disney Animation’s latest, Hexed , which is all about a mother and her teen daughter at its core against a backdrop of a world of witches. The 29-year-old has shared before that the role came at a time where a story about “an overprotective mother makes a hell of a lot more sense to me” than it would have before this phase of her life.

Outside of her latest role, Steinfeld is confirmed to reprise her role as Kate Bishop in Avengers: Doomsday , hitting theaters on December 18. Then we’ll hear her voice again as Gwen Stacy/Spider-Gwen in Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse coming out on June 18. We’re so curious what’s next for Steinfeld in her new mom era! For now, she’s staying booked and busy even as she enjoys some much-deserved time off with her baby daughter, Harper Haize Allen.

articles.title: Even Sienna Miller Was Surprised by That 'War' Ending
articles.summary: The female lead of the HBO/Sky legal drama's first season, who is no stranger to weathering tabloid scrutiny herself, opens up to THR about who came out on top in the high-profile divorce in the end.
articles.content:
[This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the War finale.]

Sienna Miller doesn’t quite know why she keeps getting tapped to play women caught up in the public eye. Since breaking out two decades ago as Edie Sedgwick in Factory Girl , the American-born English actress has made a speciality out of portraying women navigating intense media scrutiny — from Alfred Hitchcock’s tormented muse Tippi Hedren in The Girl to the embattled political wives of Showtime’s The Loudest Voice and Netflix’s Anatomy of a Scandal .

“I think it’s less that I’m seeking out these roles and more that those are the roles that people see me as, probably because a famous actress is part of my identity in a way [but] I don’t feel is part of me,” Miller tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent video call from her home in the U.K. “I feel like an actor who’s not very famous — and a mom. But it’s quite funny to perhaps send myself up by playing heightened versions of whatever I imagine people might assume that to be.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories TV All's Fair in Love and 'War': Creator George Kay Explains His Ruling on Morgan and Carla's Divorce TV Archie Renaux on 'War's Resident -- and Misunderstood -- Bad Boy

Miller’s latest TV role is no exception. In creator George Kay’s HBO/Sky legal anthology drama War , which just aired its finale on Thursday in the U.S., Miller plays film star Clara Duval, whose messy, high-profile divorce from Dominic West’s billionaire tech founder Morgan Henderson becomes a feeding frenzy for both the press and their ruthless legal teams. At the center of the dispute is an equitable split of Zephyr — the ostensibly “less toxic” social media platform that Morgan built after watching Carla endure relentless online bullying and that Carla named after Mary Darby Robinson’s poem “Ode to the Muse.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Though their lawyers push them toward scorched-earth tactics to win at all costs, the pair ultimately choose to settle on their own terms, resulting in a surprisingly optimistic portrait of life after separation. “I think the normalizing of divorce is something that should be more commonplace in the world. It doesn’t have to be hell,” Miller says. “I thought that the ending was very poignant and sweet.”

In the wide-ranging chat below, Miller opens up to THR about shedding her own people-pleasing tendencies to play a “narcissistic” (but surprisingly sympathetic) actress, why she thinks Carla really came out on top in the divorce — and how she reflects now on her own experience of being tabloid fodder in her 20s: “I’m more in a kind of anthropological way interested in it [now], because I feel maybe from some PTSD that I am separate from it.”

War creator George Kay has said he wanted an actual movie star to play Carla, but he very intentionally did not want to let any of your own personal experiences influence the writing of the character. In hindsight, what did you find most appealing about embodying someone in an esoteric world that you already know so intimately yourself?

I signed on before I knew what it was, because I only read the pilot, so I was learning on the job very much with this. This isn’t a limited series, but for me, it was. [ Writer’s note: Kay confirmed to THR that each season of War will center on a new legal dispute, with the parties being represented by the same group of lawyers at rival London firms Cathcarts & Sons and Taylor & Byrne. ] blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Sometimes when you do a limited series, you have all eight episodes and you can kind of map something out. But with this, I wouldn’t find out till a few days before we’d start shooting the next block [when] we’d get scripts. So it wasn’t that I made a choice to play somebody in those circumstances, and I don’t know now that I need to do it again. But while I was in it and learning who she was as we were going along, I thought it was interesting to feel like somebody very different in those somewhat familiar circumstances. But I think Carla’s much more steely and less naive than I am.

I wouldn’t want to describe Carla as a narcissist, but she certainly comes across as a little high-strung and self-centered.

No, she’s a narcissist. ( Laughs. )

Where do you think her narcissistic nature comes from? Did you establish any kind of backstory that could shed light on what makes her tick?

I think she’s an insecure woman who has had to deal with underestimation, and I don’t think there was one inciting incident. I think you are either one of two personality types — you either have more of a narcissistic personality, or you’re more of an empathetic person. I, as myself, would walk into a room and be concerned or pretty much aware of everybody within that room, and roughly have a temperature gauge on all of them. With Carla, I think she has decided that she’s the most important person in that room, and she doesn’t feel the need to check in with others. I think she channeled whatever abandonment she experienced into that way of being as a defense mechanism, versus my equivalent — which is exhausting, but is also a defense mechanism. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

[Playing] that was really fun. Once I made that decision to be like, “She’s not concerned with other people’s feelings or energies, and she’s very much orbiting herself” — it was so uncomfortable at first to be that way. And then anytime I stumbled upon something that my instinct would be to correct, I was like, “No, she wouldn’t bother her.” And then it was quite a liberating choice.

George has also talked about how you brought an unexpected softness to Carla that was not always part of his original conception of the character. Were there any particular moments in the season that you wanted to soften her a little bit or make her more likeable? Did you ever push back on some of her actions or decisions?

I didn’t feel like I needed to make her more likable. I sometimes needed reasons for the decisions about how she was [acting]. I felt like I really pushed back against the kind of hysterical breakdown on the talk show [in episode five], although people really enjoyed that, because I just didn’t want it to fall into any kind of “hysterical woman” trope situation. I didn’t want Morgan to appear reasonable and Carla to appear unhinged, but that’s often the way the world sees these relationships and sees the dynamics between a couple. If she’s ambitious or if she’s ruthless, she’s a bitch; if he is [those same things], he’s a great businessman. I think it does kick up some of those tropes, which I was really trying to push back on until I realized, “Well, maybe it’s a great mirror to see how women are treated and judged.” Obviously, it gets rectified, and she wins that particular battle. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

But there were moments in this that I was trying to advocate for her to be more vulnerable, or more soft, or just more three-dimensional. But then if I didn’t find it, I would just lean into her being really unashamedly a bitch or whatever she is. The moment where she couldn’t remember her son’s age — I was like, “That’s a huge thing [to forget]!” And we were learning this as we were going on. I’m like, “Does she not know her son’s age?” And then I would talk to other cast [members] who were like, “Actually, it’s kind of funny. Just do it.” But I was trying to fight for her a bit in moments.

Even though you and Dominic play the leads of this season, your characters don’t actually spend a lot of time together because they’re always busy strategizing with their own lawyers. What did all of the brief glimpses of Carla and Morgan — in the back of a limousine, in an elevator, in the back alley of the courthouse waiting for their cars in the rain — reveal to you about the nature of their relationship?

I think the thing that Carla and Morgan were missing was time together, and time and energy spent on each other. When they’re forced into those situations, other than the car at the very beginning, I think they realized that there was so much there that was probably salvageable or that they cared about. And once you get into a war situation and it’s you versus them, it’s very easy to forget those moments, the good things. But I think what probably comes across in those poignant moments is a sense of love buried underneath all of it, or consideration at least, or some form of emotion, which I think the lawyers are very good at hiding from you. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid5' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Carla’s relationship with Morgan is also very much shaped by their own financial circumstances — he is now a billionaire tech founder, and she has been experiencing a lull in her acting career and a significant dip in her income.

I think through the process of divorce and how acrimonious that is and how savage it is, you can either really sink into the resentment and the loathing, or you can remember what it was that brought you together. In the cross-examination [during the last two episodes], we’re talking about moments when we first met. Parts of it are quite therapeutic for them.

I think she genuinely feels entitled to something for Zephyr. I think she really does feel like she contributed more than he is allowing to be let on to the formation of that company, but she’s just vengeful. I don’t even know that it was ever about the money. I think she was just unhappy and he was unhappy, and then it got ugly. She kind of made it ugly, but that’s because she was convinced he cheated. It’s a whole mess, but there are threads within it that I also struggle to follow. So I put it down to just them being erratic and love not being a linear thing.

Carla and Morgan clearly could have settled their divorce at any point during mediation or arbitration, but it’s not until the end of their two-day trial that they decide to reach a fair settlement on their own terms without any outside intervention. In their last scene together, the two of them share a lovely moment on the beach in Normandy, and they are last seen walking back to her cottage to have a hot chocolate with Gabe (Aran Murphy, son of Cilian), Carla’s son from a previous relationship. What did you make of the resolution of their relationship? blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid6' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I think they’re both battle-weary by that point, and they’ve seen all of the duplicity amongst the legal teams, and that side of things is so ugly. They’ve humiliated each other publicly and been backed into corners, and I think they don’t recognize themselves in some of those moments. I found I was expecting more fireworks at the ending. ( Laughs. ) And then in reflection, I think the normalizing of divorce is something that should be more commonplace in the world. It doesn’t have to be hell. I thought that the ending was very poignant and sweet.

Basically, what happened was that Dom and I never really got to work together. So anytime we did, we were very happy, which I think serves the story and adds a little sort of something to the scenes. But I found that scene on the beach touching to shoot and surprisingly emotional. But again, there are so many different ways that this could have gone, and I have to defer to the writing team to come up with the best one. I think Carla should have won! I probably was drawn to it becoming more ugly. But actually, the lawyers are the ugly people, and that’s the moral of the story. Even though Carla and Morgan are also ugly and narcissistic. ( Laughs. )

What do you think it says about us as a culture that we immediately think of the worst possible scenario for a high-profile divorce?

Well, I don’t know. I think it’s wealthy people. We want to see them being treated like normal people, being dragged through the mud. It’s the same with Succession . We loved watching those people get it wrong and fall apart. I think there must be some kind of schadenfreude. It’s wonderful to be in those aspirational worlds and then wonderful to be reminded that, irrespective of how aspirational this world is or how great it looks from the outside, they’re two people dealing with shit. It’s just with many more zeros on the end of it. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid7' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

George has told me his theory about what happens to Carla and Morgan’s relationship, but what do you imagine Carla and Morgan’s lives — either together or apart — will look like going forward?

I think they’ll be really good friends, but I think he will regret [the divorce] more than she will. So that’s me defending my character, and Dom would say the same thing about his. ( Laughs. )

Over the last couple of decades, you have played a lot of women — and particularly actresses — who are navigating intense public scrutiny. It’s hard not to think about how the early years of your career in the mid-2000s were overshadowed by British tabloid culture and paparazzi obsession. How do you reflect now on the harsh treatment that you endured in your 20s?

Yeah, it feels so alien to the world that we live in now that it’s almost comical. It’s not comical, but I’m baffled that that existed. The ’90s [had] a lad culture in England, and God forbid, you couldn’t take the piss out of yourself and laugh at yourself. If you couldn’t laugh at yourself or send yourself up, you weren’t worth talking to in England. So I think I kind of absorbed that lad culture and was quite gobby and probably quite fun for them fodder-wise. But the lad culture meant that the paparazzi were just ravenous and unstoppable and aggressive and violent, and it’s just so different to the world [now]. It just would not be allowed; it wouldn’t be tolerated. People on the street wouldn’t stand for it if they saw what was happening. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid8' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

It was young women that were targeted and cameras up your skirts — just shocking. But you look back and you’re like, “God, that’s not long ago,” and it was absolutely accepted and paid for and devoured. So I’m more in a kind of anthropological way interested in it [now], because I feel maybe from some PTSD that I am separate from it. I can look back on it with curiosity and philosophy versus trauma and just be like, “God, that’s crazy that it wasn’t that long ago, and that’s how we lived.” But pre-social media, in 2008, the whole world shifted. In 2012, it really shifted, but it’s just interesting to look back on that time and to have been such a part of it and feel like it’s so foreign. I think it was too much for anyone to really live like 15 people outside your house and chasing you everywhere you went. I’ve always been the same — I’m quite a normal, grounded person that it just didn’t suit [my life]. I don’t want bodyguards and putting on makeup every day.

You’ve spoken about wanting to take yourself more seriously as an actress, and reaching a point in your life where you are decidedly less interested in hearing other people’s opinions. When did that shift start for you?

I think I always took my work really seriously. I just think it was a battle to be seen as a serious actor in my 20s, but we are way beyond that now. I think when I had my first daughter, life just suddenly felt more serious, and the choices that I was making, they had to be worthy of being away from home and taking my kid on the road, and there was just more levity to each decision. articles.title: Danny Boyle on 'Ink' and Murdoch, the 'Trainspotting' Toilet Scene and How 'Slumdog Millionaire' Almost Went Straight to Video
articles.summary: The Oscar-winning filmmaker spoke with The Hollywood Reporter in front of an audience at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, where he was honored with the Maverick Director Award.
articles.content:
"Decades before clickbait, before Fox News, before OnlyFans, before Truth Social, before Google, before Facebook, before any of it , something started that we're still living with the consequences of," Danny Boyle said while recording an episode of The Hollywood Reporter ’s Awards Chatter podcast in front of an audience at the recent SCAD Savannah Film Festival , where he was being honored with the fest's Maverick Director Award. The Oscar-winning director was referring to the fateful 1969 meeting of Australian businessman Rupert Murdoch and British newspaperman Larry Lamb, and the tabloid journalism that it spawned, which is chronicled in Boyle's latest film, Ink , which Netflix will release in theaters on Dec. 11 and on its streaming platform on Jan. 8. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories SCAD Savannah Film Festival 'American Doctor' Director on Her Powerful Gaza Doc: "I Wanted to Do Something" Movies Ron Howard Wasn't Sure He Was the Right Director for 'Avedon'; This Is What Changed His Mind

The 70-year-old Englishman has directed 15 features over the past 32 years, including 1994's Shallow Grave , 1996's Trainspotting , 2002's 28 Days Later , 2008's Slumdog Millionaire , 2010's 127 Hours and 2015's Steve Jobs . Described by the New York Times as “a cinematic hypnotist” and by The Guardian as “a film director in a class of his own,” he won best director Academy, Golden Globe and BAFTA awards for Slumdog , and an Emmy for his work on the London 2012 Olympic Games Opening Ceremony. And he also was presented with a Britannia Award for Artistic Excellence in 2009 and a BFI Fellowship in 2010.

You can watch the listen to or watch the entire episode above, or read select excerpts below…

On the scene in Trainspotting in which Ewan McGregor swims through "the worst toilet in Scotland"…

"CG was just beginning to emerge in cinemas. In fact, there was a Christmas film out at the time with Tim Allen playing Santa Clause, and they squeezed him into a chimney pot. That's one of the very first uses of CG in film. It looked terrible, I thought. I thought, 'We're not going to do it like that,' because somebody said, 'Oh, you could use CG,' as it was at the time. We wanted to do it live. So we used a theater trick, the trompe l'oeil: you cut the toilet in half and film it from the side. So, obviously, it isn't a toilet on this side; it's the slide that McGregor goes down. Then Brian [Tufano, the cinematographer] told Ewan [McGregor, the film's star] to twist his feet 'round at the end, because then people will think it's the U-bend that you're going 'round, which curiously people do. It's just that illusion that we buy into. If you believe the actors, you'll believe anything! So people believed it was the worst toilet in Scotland, even though it smelled of chocolate, because all the shit was chocolate, and it was delicious! All the prop girls had candles burning so that everybody felt good about being there all day." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

On how Slumdog Millionaire almost went straight-to-video instead of to the Oscars…

"There was a change of regime at Warner Bros., and there was a change of emphasis. They decided that films that they put a bit of money up for would not be worth the cost of releasing, so they decided to put them straight out on video. And it wasn't just my film, there was a Guy Ritchie film as well, Revolver , and a couple of others like that, as well. Fortunately, Peter Rice, [who was running Fox Searchlight at the time and] who's just taken over Netflix, picked it up and bought it off Warners, which normally doesn't happen. He knew somehow that when you played it with an audience, it would prove itself."

"The film's really about truth, so you have to tell the truth about Murdoch and what Murdoch was like. Even though people would prefer you to paint him as a villain, he, in fact, had many reservations about what was going on. But he didn't act on them, which is as much condemnation as you need, I think, rather than just portraying him as a villain."

"He is the kind of actor like [Al] Pacino is, who can take you to an impossibly dark place — in Pacino's case, the ordering of the execution of his brother [in The Godfather, Part II ] — and yet you still lean into the character. Jack has that. If you think about he stuff he does in Sinners and in 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple , he's a monster, and yet you're drawn into him. That's a weird duality he has, which not many actors do. He's a wonderful, wonderful actor."

articles.title: On This Day in 1963, Doctor Who Made Its TV Debut & But a Chaotic Week in Britain Almost Ruined the Premiere
articles.summary: While most UK TV premieres enjoy an easy ride onto the air, there are exceptions—and the lead-up to Doctor Who was more like a rollercoaster than an easy cruise. Yeesh. And on November 23, 1963, nobody could have envisaged what a hit the strange new sci-fi series would become. You might think the show's legacy […]
articles.content:
Add Us On Google While most UK TV premieres enjoy an easy ride onto the air, there are exceptions—and the lead-up to Doctor Who was more like a rollercoaster than an easy cruise. Yeesh. And on November 23, 1963, nobody could have envisaged what a hit the strange new sci-fi series would become. You might think the show's legacy started smoothly, but nope, it was anything but. Unfortunately, the very first episode was caught up in a storm of production problems and unpredictable events.

The path to TV for the Doctor was not an easy one. The BBC faced unexpected obstacles, and the first episode did not air as planned. The results got so knotted up that the BBC figured audiences deserved a second chance to see the start of this remarkable story. An appropriately strange beginning for a series that would go on to spend decades defying reality until it all seemed quite normal.

Before Doctor Who became a beloved fixture of pop culture, getting its very first episode on air was a very real challenge. The first version of "An Unearthly Child" was recorded back in September 1963, but it wasn't quite up to the BBC's high standards. Technical difficulties and concerns about the cast's performances left the production team unhappy with the results. Rather than simply accept the recording and move forward, the decision was made to reshoot the episode. That meant bringing the cast and crew back together to do it all over again. It must have felt like an ironic time-travel job for the series. Fortunately, the second recording proved more successful, and the BBC managed to get the episode ready for its scheduled November premiere.

However, everything that followed was upstaged by other events. On November 22, 1963, the world was shocked into silence when President John F. Kennedy was tragically assassinated in Dallas, Texas. News of the shooting was broadcast on television screens across the world, and the BBC, which had devoted plenty of airtime to the tragedy, ended up overshadowing the new Doctor Who series. The show was forced to make its debut the following day with much less fanfare than intended. To make matters worse, there were technical difficulties, too, as some regions experienced power failures, meaning viewers couldn't watch the episode when it was being broadcast. For a series that would become a TV mainstay for decades to come, its first leap through history was anything but smooth.

All was not lost, however. When it became clear after the turmoil of the first airing that many viewers hadn't had a chance to experience the series' first adventure, the BBC decided to give them another opportunity. With extensive coverage of Kennedy's assassination and widespread problems with the electricity supply, the network hadn't successfully introduced the series to the world in the way it had hoped. And so, instead of simply plowing on and blindly trusting that viewers would catch up, the BBC issued an extra broadcast of "An Unearthly Child" on November 30, 1963. This gave audiences a second chance to meet the mysterious Doctor, his granddaughter, and the two unlikely schoolteachers caught up in one of the most extraordinary adventures of all time.

That repeat also gave the series another chance to establish its wonderfully bizarre concept. When teachers Ian Chesterton and Barbara Wright become interested in their student Susan's strange knowledge, which seems to go far beyond anything an ordinary schoolgirl should know, their investigation leads them to a strange police box and its equally odd owner. Soon, they're leaping through space and time in the TARDIS, and the longest-running saga in television history has begun. Nobody involved in those original broadcasts could have known just how successful the show would become. What started as a small BBC science-fiction story would eventually turn into a television juggernaut, with a new Doctor for each successive generation. And when the original series eventually had to return to its own beginnings, the fact that it all started with a second chance seems more appropriate than you might think for a Time Lord.

articles.title: Disney's Doomsday Essential MCU Watch List Proves Marvel Hasn't Learned Its Lesson
articles.summary: Now that Avengers: Doomsday is getting closer and closer, fans of the Marvel Cinematic Universe are rewatching past movies and TV shows in preparation for the blockbuster. Playing into that, Disney has gone out of their way to release a list of projects that you should watch before you hit the theater for Avengers: Doomsday. […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Now that Avengers: Doomsday is getting closer and closer, fans of the Marvel Cinematic Universe are rewatching past movies and TV shows in preparation for the blockbuster. Playing into that, Disney has gone out of their way to release a list of projects that you should watch before you hit the theater for Avengers: Doomsday . It's bigger than any previous watchlist concept due to the sheer size of the cast and how far back things go, with some of the heroes in the film making their debut more than 25 years ago. In fact, the watchlist starts with 2000's X-Men .

There's also the sequel to that movie, Captain America: The First Avenger , three Avengers films, Spider-Man: No Way Home , Loki, Thunderbolts*, The Fantastic Four: First Steps , and more. You can watch Avengers: Doomsday without seeing all these movies and shows and still have a great time, but making sure you check these out will enhance your viewing experience. While that might sound like a good idea in practice, it's something that has caused issues for the MCU in the past, so it's surprising to see the franchise leaning so heavily into basically assigning homework for so many of its viewers, which could be a mistake.

The films and television shows that are officially on the essential watchlist ahead of Avengers: Doomsday are X-Men, X2, Captain America: The First Avenger, The Avengers, Avengers: Infinity War, Avengers: Endgame, Loki, Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, Spider-Man: No Way Home, Black Panther: Wakanda Forever, Captain America: Brave New World, Deadpool & Wolverine, Thunderbolts* , and The Fantastic Four: First Steps . That is a lot to digest and would take around two days or more to complete. That's not even to mention things like VisionQuest , which is also important after its post-credit scene involving Doctor Doom .

As fun as it is to watch these projects again, that does feel like a lot of homework. It also spans such a long time that it shows just how much content is going to be in Avengers: Doomsday . It shouldn't take that long to prepare for one single film, no matter how big it is. Despite that lengthy endeavor, it still also feels like a relatively incomplete list. A film like The Marvels isn't included, even though it featured a scene where Monica Rambeau ended up in a universe with Beast from the Fox X-Men movies. That either means the list is wrong or that The Marvels is actually not important, which is disappointing.

Ultimately, giving the audience a lot of things to keep track of feels like a mistake. Although a franchise being as interconnected as the MCU is appealing and part of why it has the level of success that it does, things may have expanded a bit too far. Since the days of Avengers: Doomsday , many fans have kind of checked out of the MCU and a common reason is that it has become too much to keep track of. That's especially true now that Fox properties like the X-Men have been woven into things.

It's hard for anyone who isn't fully immersed in the franchise to also do the same. This has actually caused problems for some MCU movies of the 2020s. Captain America: Brave New World was a box office disappointment and a big reason why was that it was basically a sequel to 2008's The Incredible Hulk , which most people don't care about. You also needed some knowledge of the forgettable Eternals. As fun as it is, The Marvels is the biggest bomb in MCU history , which was partially caused by having to know about Captain Marvel, Ms. Marvel, and WandaVision . Meanwhile, Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania needed you to know what happened in Loki to fully grasp the villain.

Thunderbolts* , which is still on the essential watchlist, struggled commercially, and you had to have seen Black Widow, Hawkeye, Ant-Man and the Wasp, The Falcon and the Winter Soldier , and more to understand every element. Even if everything in the MCU is great, that's a lot to ask of casual moviegoers. The fact that it derailed several projects, yet it's being used as a selling point for Avengers: Doomsday shows that Marvel hasn't really learned its lesson. It could be a case where the franchise is just so confident in the Avengers name that they think it can't be derailed. It'll be interesting to see how it performed compared to previous Avengers projects.

Are you going to watch everything on this watchlist? Do you think it's a good idea or a bad idea? Let us know in the comments!

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Avengers: Doomsday released its final trailer today, and it finally revealed more about the heart of the story and the deeper motivations of the many Marvel characters that are appearing in the movie. However, all that new footage is providing more and more clues for dedicated fans to piece together, and you better believe that's exactly what's happening.

One fan took to Reddit to show their fan-edit work, which pieces together seemingly different scenes of Avengers: Doomsday into a full scene of events that transpire between some key leaders of the heroes and Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.). However, if this Doomsday fan edit is correct, it corroborates some of the biggest leaks about the film's story and the major twist in its approach to the Marvel Cinematic Universe version of Doom.

The fan-edit video isn't perfect, but it captures the gist of what happens at this pivotal point in Avengers: Doomsday . If you want to look over the details, set in proper order, then read the possible SPOILERS , below.

There are, of course, a lot of fine details in between these plot points that would need to be explained. And, as stated, even the Reddit video doesn't have the sequence of events entirely right. However, everything described above can be backed up by the other trailers and behind-the-scenes videos that Marvel Studios has released, and soft-confirming that Doom pulls a wolf in sheep's clothing move on the heroes may other leaks sound more credible. That includes the theory that Doom uses Tony Stark's likeness to earn the trust of the MCU Avengers – a trick we may have seen him pulling at the end of Fantastic Four: First Steps , when he is interacting (maskless) with Franklin Richards, whose reality-altering powers could change Doom facial appearance in an instant.

There is also the question of what Doom may have done to Earth-10005 that caused the level of destruction that we see on that battlefiled, which prompts Reed Richards to scream "Did you do this?!" in Doom's face. Other rumors have said senior characters like Patrick Stewart's Professor X and Ian McKellen's Magneto may be the first ones Doom takes out, to steal both of their powers. That would explain how those Sentinels get raised from the ground (Doom using Magneto's powers).

The risk in this approach is clear, though: Avengers: Doomsday would be walking a tightrope of dramatic irony: everyone in the audience will have to still sympathize with watching the heroes hanging out with a guy named "Doom," totally oblivious to the fact that he might be a threat, based solely on a face-card. Suddenly Star-Lord's Thanos blunder wouldn't look like the dumbest moment in MCU risk-prevention ever.

Avengers: Doomsday will be released in theaters on December 18th. Do you think this theory is on the money?
