articles.title: Cyberpunk 2 Director Jokes That the Sequel is Now Canceled, And GTA 6 Is to Blame
articles.summary: Courtesy of CD Projekt Red The release of GTA 6 may impact the sequel to Cyberpunk 2077, in spite of the jokes the Cyberpunk 2 director has made about the game being cancelled due to Rockstar's incredibly successful title launch. The impressive nature of GTA 6 has caused Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzyński to go into something they call […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The release of GTA 6 may impact the sequel to Cyberpunk 2077 , in spite of the jokes the Cyberpunk 2 director has made about the game being cancelled due to Rockstar's incredibly successful title launch. The impressive nature of GTA 6 has caused Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzyński to go into something they call a " GTA 6 -induced-open-world-game-dev-depression," joking about how high the game's quality is as a fellow creative and artist. Also describing Rockstar's game as a "technological and creative miracle," the cancellation of Cyberpunk 2 may hold some real merit as design ideas get updated to take ideas from GTA 6 .

Obviously, Cyberpunk 2 isn't actually cancelled , as the game has been in development since at least May 2025 following an announcement of it being green lit with studio CD Projekt Red. However, now that GTA 6 has changed the landscape of open-world sandbox experiences similar to Cyberpunk 2077 , production timelines may change at CD Projekt Red to reflect the immersive depth of Rockstar's megahit. At the very least, this acknowledgment from one of gaming's most respected development groups could be healthy for the industry as a whole, showing the beginning of new trends other games try to adopt from GTA 6 's formula.

Sarzyński isn't the only director at CD Projekt Red to give GTA 6 its flowers, as associate game director Paweł Sasko has called the title a "generational banger" among other praise. One of the co-founders of the company have also given positive statements on GTA 6 , with joint CEO Michał Nowakowski congratulating the team at Rockstar for the release of such a huge project. While the jokes about cancellation from Sarzyński clearly aren't literal, it's clear that CD Projekt Red's creative minds are looking at GTA 6 extensively, perhaps picking up inspirations for Cyberpunk 2 that players might want to see.

Investors will always chase trends, so it won't be a surprise when some games try to reflect everything GTA 6 does without realizing the amount of time, dedication, and effort that was required to turn a $1 billion project into a stellar game. There is a small chance that CD Projekt Red's backers will feel this way, trying to mold Cyberpunk 2 into something that mirrors Rockstar's design philosophy for GTA 6 . Yet, whether this does happen or not, the impact from GTA 6 could cause some changes in game direction or roadmaps, causing the initial development of Cyberpunk 2 to grow longer as CD Projekt Red takes their new inspirations into account.

Despite how players may not like the time between Cyberpunk 2077 and its sequel growing longer, it might be for the best. GTA 6 has a level of engaging detail in its map that makes it astounding, giving players endless encounters and interactions to make the setting feel like a living, breathing world. From dynamic NPC conversations to reputation, physical health, and relationship systems, GTA 6 can sink players into its world with ease. That approach is something Cyberpunk 2 can do to improve upon its already great predecessor, making a deeper sandbox with all the same dystopian sci-fi flair that the original established.

Thankfully, Igor Sarzyński goes on past his cancellation joke to say that Cyberpunk 2 is something unique on its own, while GTA 6 's dedication to its vision is just as noteworthy as any specific system. Sarzyński says that "I think we're doing something of our own, with a different unique flavor. GTA 6 is impressive in a way all great art is, it expands what is possible, a captivating vision flawlessly executed." The scale of GTA 6 simply isn't feasible for any game project, even if investors insist on creating a project with the same fidelity and depth of detail.

It would be foolish for CD Projekt Red to drop everything they've already built to chase GTA 6 's design in a 1:1 style. That would be similar to the awful trend of games constantly chasing Fortnite by adding some type of live service or monetization through multiplayer, which has caused games like Anthem , Highguard , Concord , and many others to fail. While we will undoubtedly see some games in the next few years try to copy GTA 6 , it would be better for games to take the right lessons from it instead. Greater immersive quality to game worlds and a commitment to a engaging, non-linear sandbox should be something new projects adopt, not just having huge populations of NPCs or life-sim mechanics.

Hopefully, CD Projekt Red's appreciation for GTA 6 comes from how the game opened their eyes to new possibilities within their own titles. With The Witcher 4 on its way to deliver an equally detailed fantasy RPG world, perhaps the future of Cyberpunk can depend on the right pieces of influence from Rockstar. We have no idea what a sequel to Cyberpunk 2077 will look like, but in a few years, the connections to GTA 6 may be clear in the best ways.

What lessons do you want Cyberpunk 2 to take from GTA 6 ? Let us know in the comments below!

articles.content:
The 12th Cairo Film Connection , the pitching platform of the Cairo Film Festival , handed out 53 awards worth a combined $410,000 to Arab film projects at the end of its industry sidebar, Cairo Industry Days . The awards included 17 cash grants, 31 in-kind awards and five invitations to international film markets and labs, marking a significant increase in support from previous editions.

This year’s CFC brought together 17 projects from 12 countries, spanning fiction and documentary films in development and post-production. The platform hosted 104 one-on-one meetings between filmmakers and regional and international industry representatives. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories NBCUniversal, Hornbill Capital Back EloElo, Parent of Indian Microdrama Platform Story TV, in $80 Million Funding Round India's T-Series and Hungama Launch Microdrama Platform FastTV With $32 Million Commitment (EXCLUSIVE)

Palestinian filmmaker Shayma’ Awawdeh’s “The Story of the Mountain” and Syrian director Anas Zwahri’s “Their Ghosts Never Left My Home” received CFC’s two $10,000 jury awards for development and post-production, respectively. The Qatar Film Committee awarded four $25,000 grants to “Twelve Fig Leaves,” “Reda,” “Madness and Honey Days” and “Naydalaan.”

Other projects secured a combination of cash grants, technical services and invitations to international markets, including Cannes’ Fantastic 7, Durban FilmMart and Medimed.

Here is a closer look at some of the projects presented at this year’s Cairo Film Connection.

“The Story of the Mountain” (Shayma’ Awawdeh, Palestine, France. Produced by Shayma’ Awawdeh)

What would Palestinian children do if they could make the checkpoint separating their neighborhood from the rest of Hebron disappear? That question lies at the heart of “The Story of the Mountain,” a hybrid documentary in which children use filmmaking and fantasy to conceive of a reality different from their own. During a creative workshop, they imagine a magical mountain that transforms into a giant grandmother capable of destroying the checkpoint at the entrance to their neighborhood. Their fantasy becomes a way of envisioning a future free from the constraints of life under occupation. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Awawdeh, whose short documentary “ Intersecting Memory ” opened IDFA in 2025 and won Clermont-Ferrand’s Grand Prix National in 2026, is seeking co-production partners and writing residencies.

“Twelve Fig Leaves” (Joëlle Abou Chabké, Lebanon. Produced by Lara Abou Saïfan)

In Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, filmmaker Joëlle Abou Chabké is exploring an ancestral method of weather prediction. Her documentary “Twelve Fig Leaves” follows her as she tests the Bawāhīr, a traditional Lebanese practice, while building a sustainable farm with her husband in his native village. The project explores the relationship between land, heritage and belonging amid political and environmental uncertainty.

“This film lives at the intersection of climate collapse, war, ancestral knowledge and the deeply human need to belong somewhere,” Abou Chabké says.

Produced by Lara Abou Saïfan’s Placeless Films (“ Dead Dog ”), the documentary received a $25,000 Qatar Film Committee grant, following AFAC development funding and a DocsBarcelona Pro Shared Shores Award at Beirut-based Aflamuna Connection.

“Naydalaan” (Mariam Al-Dhubhani, Yemen, Jordan. Produced by Bassam Alasad)

Drawing on her childhood experiences of sleep paralysis, Yemeni filmmaker Mariam Al-Dhubhani blends fantasy and psychological horror in “Naydalaan,” a feature set in 1990s Sana’a. The story follows 10-year-old Nadia into a nightmarish world where she encounters girls from different periods of Yemen’s history, confronting questions of identity, exclusion and belonging.

“At a time when so much of Yemen is seen through destruction, I want to make room for its imagination, complexity and the many ways of belonging within it,” Al-Dhubhani says.

The project received a $25,000 Qatar Film Committee grant and $10,000 in casting and sound-mixing services. Previously developed through the Doha Film Institute’s Feature Script Lab, it is seeking further financing and international co-producers.

“The Schoolyard” (Mohamed Siam, Egypt, Belgium. Produced by Mohamed Siam and Brandy Miller)

Five teenage boys navigate friendship, violence and shifting loyalties over the course of a turbulent school year in “The Schoolyard,” a fiction feature set in a crumbling public school on Cairo’s outskirts. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“I learned early that the real lessons were often not in the classroom, but in power, fear, hierarchy and survival,” says director Mohamed Siam, who attended private, public and military schools in Egypt. Drawing on those experiences, he aims to capture “the humor, tenderness and imagination” that persist even in oppressive environments, exploring what happens when children are forced to grow up too soon.

The project received a $10,000 cash award from ART, $30,000 in technical and development services and an invitation to Durban FilmMart. Shooting is planned for summer 2027.

Siam’s previous films include “ Amal ,” which opened IDFA in 2017 and won the Golden Tanit at Carthage, and “My Father’s Scent,” which received multiple awards at Venice’s Final Cut program in 2024.

“The Man Who Is Gone” (Naji Ismail, Egypt. Produced by Muhammad Taymour)

Haunted by recurring nightmares and a deep sense of loss, a man in his 40s travels to Upper Egypt to fulfill his ailing mother’s wishes in “The Man Who Is Gone.” What begins as a family obligation takes a supernatural turn as he encounters a world of folklore and buried memories. Drawing on Upper Egypt’s traditions of myth and oral storytelling, writer and director Naji Ismail explores how grief shapes our relationship with the past, blurring the boundaries between the living and the dead.

“At a time when we are often overwhelmed by the urgency of the present, returning to these inherited stories can remind us of the depth of our human experience and our place within a much longer history,” he tells Variety .

The project received $9,000 in cash awards, additional development and post-production services and an invitation to Cannes’ Fantastic 7. Previously supported by the Doha Film Institute, it is targeting a late 2027 shoot.

“Dwellers of the Cabins” (Hend Bakr, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar. Produced by Hend Bakr and Tamer Nady)

Egyptian filmmaker Hend Bakr examines her Nubian heritage in “Dwellers of the Cabins,” a documentary about a community in Alexandria whose ancestors were displaced from southern Egypt in the early 20th century. Now threatened with demolition to make way for an investment project, the settlement where Bakr grew up has become the focus of her efforts to preserve her community’s history. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“I am telling my own story and the struggle of my own family between preserving their culture and being included,” Bakr says.

The documentary received $15,000 in sound and DCP mastering services and an invitation to Rough Cut Lab Africa. With approximately 30% of its financing secured, the project is targeting completion in 2028.

“Terminus” (Oumaima Trabelsi, Tunisia. Produced by Oumaima Trabelsi and Erige Sehiri)

Ten years after being deported from Italy, Sadok spends his days driving his taxi along the same 10-kilometer route through the Tunisian hometown he once hoped to escape. His repetitive journeys form the basis of “Terminus,” a documentary exploring the tension between returning home and the lingering desire to build a life elsewhere.

“At a time when migration is often told through the act of leaving, I want to turn my gaze towards what comes after, and what remains of that longing once the journey is over,” director Oumaima Trabelsi says.

The project received a $1,000 development award and $15,000 in sound and subtitling services. Previously supported by Tunisia’s Ministry of Culture, it is targeting completion in January 2028.

“Dear Tarkovsky” (Firas Khoury, Sweden, Jordan, France. Produced by Linda Mutawi)

Palestinian filmmaker Firas Khoury, whose debut feature “ Alam ” won three awards at CIFF in 2022, is developing “Dear Tarkovsky,” a tragicomedy about a filmmaker who stages a fake rescue to convince a wealthy man’s daughter to finance his debut about the acclaimed Soviet director, only to fall in love with her.

“The film is a celebration of cinema,” Khoury says. “We, as Palestinians, have the right to put our name forward as explorers in art as well, not only as humanitarian cases.”

Produced by Linda Mutawi’s Stockholm-based Fikra, the $3.5 million project previously received support from the Tunisian-Italian Fund, Malmö Industry Days and Durban FilmMart. It is seeking additional financing and co-production partners.

“Their Ghosts Never Left My Home”

(Anas Zwahri, France, Syria, Qatar, Lebanon. Produced by Ahmad Alhaj)

For five Syrian mothers whose sons were forcibly disappeared under the Assad regime, the lack of closure has become part of everyday life. “Their Ghosts Never Left My Home” explores how the women preserve their sons’ memories while continuing to seek explanations about their fates. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“Two years after the fall of the regime in Syria, the issue of the forcibly disappeared remains unaddressed,” Zwahri says. “Many families await answers from the new government, but their pleas go unanswered.”

The documentary received CFC’s $10,000 post-production jury award and festival distribution services from Cult. Supported by AFAC, Aflamuna and the Doha Film Institute, it is targeting a 2027 premiere.

“A Butterfly Hug” (Sally Abobasha, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Sweden. Produced by Aya Tallah Yusuf and Sally Abobasha)

Filmed over six years in Cairo’s working-class neighborhoods, “A Butterfly Hug” follows Sajda, Shorouk, Shahd and Abdelrahman, young people living with epidermolysis bullosa, a rare genetic condition that makes their skin extremely fragile, as they navigate adolescence, friendship and family expectations.

“What attracted me to them wasn’t their disease. It was their confidence, their laughter and their dreams,” director Sally Abobasha says. “They reminded me of myself as a teenager, although they were much braver than I was,” she adds.

The documentary, filmed in a cinéma vérité style, secured $12,000 in cash grants from AH Media, Traveler and Stars Media, alongside $30,000 in post-production services and an invitation to Medimed, with completion targeted for early 2028.

“Growing Up Twice” (Khaled Alkhaldi, Syria, Jordan. Produced by Lujain Hamdan. Co-produced by Deema Dabis)

Set between Jordan’s Za’atari refugee camp and Amman, “Growing Up Twice” follows Baraa, a young Syrian mother who survived child marriage and is struggling to reclaim her independence while raising her son. As she attempts to build a new life, family pressures and “cycles of violence” force her to confront the difficult choices between personal freedom and motherhood.

“This film became my act of rebellion, a way to turn my anger at the injustice and cruelty in this world into action,” producer Lujain Hamdan says. “As documentary filmmakers, we must learn how to approach these difficult stories and carry them to the world,” director Khaled Alkhaldi adds.

The documentary received $6,000 in post-production services from Cult. With approximately 40% of its budget secured, the filmmakers are seeking additional financing and international co-producers ahead of a planned 2028 release.

articles.title: How Iran's Pegah Ahangarani Turned Her Family Archives Into a Regime-Challenging Oscar Hopeful
articles.summary: The director of 'Rehearsals for a Revolution,' the U.K.'s submission for best international feature at the Academy Awards, on 40 years of Iranian history told through her own life — and how an exile built the film with almost no money.
articles.content:
"Cinema is not just part of my life," begins Pegah Ahangarani. "It's me, actually."

The director and actress grew up on film sets. Both of her parents were filmmakers themselves and immersed their children in the Iranian entertainment industry. Ahangarani became a child star, skyrocketing to fame at just 14 in 1999's The Girl in the Sneakers . "I won a lot of awards," she smiles to The Hollywood Reporter . But even she couldn't have predicted the award-winning success of her debut feature-length documentary, Rehearsals for a Revolution . blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Movies Record Number of International and Animated Features Oscar-Eligible This Season Music Don Toliver Postpones O2 Arena Show After Evacuation Due to "Unknown Substance" Released at Manchester Concert

The Cannes-premiering — and L'Œil d'or-winning — project is a poignant reminder of the power of memory. Ahangarani, whose other essay documentaries include shorts I Am Trying to Remember (2021), My Father (2023) and Child Soldier (2024), sketches her entire life story in this latest work. Drawing from personal archives, home videos, street protest footage, newspapers and recorded voices, she retraces more than 40 years of Iran ’s turbulent history. From the late '70s up until the war with the U.S. and Israel, Ahangarani pieces together and narrates intimate recollections from her life — the vanilla scent of her schoolteacher's hair and desperate search for her uncle in videos from the 1999 Iranian student protests among them — that help to form the portrait of a country shaped by political repression, and in constant hope for a revolution.

Personal is the operative word in this co-production between the Czech Republic and Spain. "I want to tell my audience: 'Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility,'" says its director. As daunting as that task was — Ahangarani has already been arrested and spent time in the notorious Evin Prison, and expects not to be able to return to Iran at the risk of a lengthy jail sentence following the release of this film — she remains steadfast in her belief that using family archives is the greatest weapon at her disposal against the regime. "I realized, 'Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools,'" says Ahangarani. "Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Having left Iran in 2022, Ahangarani shares candid reflections with viewers about the guilt she's experienced in the wake of this year's civilian massacres and brutal crackdown on the Woman, Life, Freedom movement back home. From London, where she has been settled since 2023, Ahangarani talks to THR about putting that guilt up on screen — and being selected as the U.K.'s submission for best international feature film at the 2027 Oscars : "When you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land… [Now], there is one place that accepted me."

You grew up in film and TV. You were a child star. But when did you first realize you'd like to direct films yourself?

I grew up in cinema, yes. All of the crew members were like my family members. I called them aunties and uncles. ( Laughs .) I cannot separate myself from cinema. Cinema is not just part of my life — it's me, actually. I started cinema as my main career when I was 14. I acted in one film, The Girl in the Sneakers , and that film became very successful. I won a lot of awards. I was a teenager, and I was super happy. And then a few years after that, I remember I saw some documentaries and I thought, "OK, I'd like to maybe be a documentary filmmaker." I made a few documentaries, but they were very naive. It [was] TV-style documentaries. Then I got familiar with [the] essay style in literature, and then I started exploring that style in some documentaries. I saw some Chris Marker documentaries for example, and Jonas Mekas. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I thought maybe I should find that style for myself, so six or seven years ago I made a short documentary with this style. I used personal archives and I used my voiceover as a narration, and I started making very personal documentaries. That film became very successful as well. The New Yorker published that documentary. It premiered at IDFA Film Festival and a lot of festivals after that. And then I made another short documentary, same style, and another one again. And then after those three documentaries, I started making this one.

The archive of film and photos you use in this is just incredible. Is it daunting, or were you nervous, crafting an entire project around such intimate artefacts and stories?

Yes, actually. ( Laughs .) I had a lot of concern about it, and not just for this film. […] A few years ago, when I was living in Iran, I went to my grandmother's house, and I found some old family albums there. And I started looking through the photographs, and then I saw one photo. My mom was there. My father was there. I was there too. I was two or three years old, and I noticed a man who was standing next to my father, but his face had been scratched out. And I asked my grandmother, "Who is this person? Why has his face been scratched out?" She said, "He was your father's best friend. He was executed after the revolution because he was a political prisoner." And I realized my grandmother didn't destroy the whole photo. She kept that photo, just scratched that face. After that shocking moment, I realized that maybe my responsibility as a documentary filmmaker is to find these old family photos, this personal footage, and find these scratched-out faces and bring them back to life, bring them back to the frame, and bring them back to our collective memory. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

After that, I thought a lot about these archives, and I realized, 'Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools.' Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe. From that day, I started thinking about how I should use these materials as my facts. […] If you go deeper [into] one photograph, if you focus on it, you can see the part of our history in that photograph. But that wasn't easy at all. When I made that short documentary, I sent it to my mother because my mother was one of the characters, my father was one of the characters, and I had a lot of concern because they might be in trouble after that film. But they were okay. I remember one thing: I sent my film to my grandmother, and I told her, "Okay, I made a short documentary based on the photo that you kept for me." And she said, "Yes, maybe I kept that photo just for you to make this documentary."

This is a co-production between Spain and the Czech Republic, is that right? What work went into getting this over the line? Because using your own photos, films and narration, it strikes me as incredibly inexpensive documentary.

[It was made] with nothing, actually. ( Laughs .) I had a producer [with whom] I made three of my short documentaries, Kaveh Farnam [founder of the Czech Republic's Media Nest], and he's an Iranian independent film [producer] outside of Iran. I remember when I was making a previous documentary, I found him, I texted him, and he joined the project. And that one was like this — I didn't need money because I worked with my personal archives. But I wanted support for distribution [and] things. At that time, I was inside Iran, and I told Mr. Farnum that after this film, if I got arrested or something like that, please publish the film. I needed someone just for publishing. And then when I moved to London, I talked to Mr. Farnum about this feature film, and he said, "Okay, I'm in," and I didn't need any money for that. I just needed a small [amount of] money for my editor [Arash Ashtiani]. The Spain company [Fasten Films]… they found me and they wanted me to make another film for them. And then I told them, "I have one film, it's finished now. I can send it to you, and if you want, you can join this project as well." They supported us because we needed some money for the copyright of the music and sound design, and they have a good relationship with a French distributor… Then they sent the film to the Cannes Film Festival, and they have a very good relationship with Cannes because they are French, and everything actually happened after that. But for the process of making this, we didn't need any money.

One standout part of the documentary, for me, is when you're scrolling through some of those harrowing images and videos from this year's protests and you talk about your guilt and trying to compensate for that with the film. What has it been like reckoning with that through these glamorous film festivals?

Everything was very strange because right after the massacre, we were in the process of editing episode five. We wanted to show me [and] my new life as an immigrant, living in exile, and then war happened and massacre happened, and so we didn't know how we should respond [to] these disasters in our film. That was a very complicated situation because I couldn't focus on the film. I told my editor, "Cinema doesn't mean [anything] anymore after all these dead bodies." And then I realized that, "Okay, I should share all these concerns with my audience because this is the only way I should tell them."

But I didn't have any idea that the the film [could] be successful. During the process of making this, it was just me and my editor, Arash, and a little mic, and a very intimate space. I remember the distribution company texted me and told me the director of Cannes, Thierry Frémaux, told us maybe you can be in the official selection. That was very exciting. That day, I just lay down on the sofa in our office… I couldn't handle this much excitement. We realized we can compete with, for example, Steven Soderbergh, because he had a film in Cannes in the official documentary selection. And in Cannes, they told us, "You won the best documentary prize," and I think I'm in the middle of some dream or something like that. What do you hope audiences are talking and thinking about after seeing this film?

After the first screening in Cannes, I realized one thing, which was very sweet: When the film finished and people started clapping, many of them came and told me, "We think we love your people as much as you." I thought, 'So this is cinema.' You can show something that people don't have any idea about, and they can resonate with it, and they can feel this struggle. They can feel [for] your people, which is amazing.

Many people, after watching the film, they think they know me very well [and that] they're a friend of mine, which is very sweet. I think the film is successful because I could create a sense of intimacy. Through the narration and through the film, I want to tell my audience: "Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility."

This film is officially the U.K.'s official Oscar submission for best international feature. What does that mean to you?

That was great news. Not just because of the film, but when you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land. When I left Iran, I thought, "OK, this is just a temporary situation." And then I realized that no, maybe it's permanent. I cannot go back anymore. I should accept my new life, and that was very difficult. When the U.K. announced that they picked our film … I had a feeling like I wasn't stateless anymore. There is one place that accepted me. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid6' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I'm sure you miss your family so much, but you don't envision a future where you can return?

When I left Iran in 2021, I didn't have any plan to stay outside of Iran. I left my country with just one carry-on to participate in the IDFA Film Festival for my short documentary. And after the second screening, my mother, she was in Iran [and] called me and told me the regime had called her and asked her to interrogate me about the film. She told me, "Stay outside for a while, for one or two months." And then the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement happened and I published a video to show my solidarity with that movement, and then my mother told me they sent a letter [saying] there is a court order against me. They seized my apartment and my bank accounts in Iran and I realized that I can't go back. If I go back, I have to go to jail. In Prime Video’s latest original Christmas romantic comedy, Clashing Through the Snow , Christopher Briney ( The Summer I Turned Pretty) and Michell Randolph ( Landman ) portray rival editors whose relationship takes an enemies to lovers arc during a road trip to New York .

Ryan Mitchell (Briney) and Hannah Hendricks both hear from their boss Jeremy (P.J. Byrne) separately that layoffs loom at Latitude Publishing, where they will compete for a merged version of their roles in the new year. The ambitious employees then both set up secret meetings with prospective authors that could respectively land them the job, but require travel to New York city over the Christmas holiday. The pair exhibit fundamentally different taste in books and what they aim to sell, but their shared love of reading provides them common ground on which to bond when a winter storm forces them together during their grounded travels to the east coast. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“Ryan's sort of an interesting case because he's obviously like, ‘How do we market this and how do we make this sellable and profitable?' But he loves books. There's a big part of his heart — and they get into it in the movie — that appreciates literature, and really he just wants people to read books,” Briney said of his character, who leans more into numbers and trends. “That's what it's about. “She’s a literary traditionalist. I remember when I first booked [the role], I was like, ‘I've got to read Virginia Woolf,’ because she talks about how that's who raised her. In the below interview, the stars also break down their reactions to the script, Briney’s Jim Carrey-like approach to physical comedy, Hannah’s career focus, working with Lukas Gage, Buc-ees knockoff Luc-ees and more:

MICHELLE RANDOLPH : I read the script multiple times before I signed on to the project. I actually I have this app called Speechify, and I remember I got the script and I was driving and I was like, 'I just really want to read it right now. 'So I listened to it for the first time with Gwyneth Paltrow reading it/speaking it to me. And then once once I got home, I sat down and I actually went through it, a very different experience, but it's such a joyful, fun script. It's silly. It's absurd. I love [that] both the characters have a real emotional core and very specific personalities. I love this script.

CHRISTOPHER BRINEY: It made me laugh, and I think it's really sweet, but I loved that that comedy was an important character in in this script, and it felt like a fun, challenging project, and it was certainly challenging and certainly fun.

DEADLINE: Chris, I feel like you really leaned into the physical comedy of this one.

BRINEY: I hope it's funny, dude. I might like look like an idiot.

DEADLINE: No, that’s not what I’m saying! Could you talk more about the challenge of that and how it was fun to explore that as an actor?

BRINEY: Yeah, I mean, it was really fun. I think that the first couple weeks on a project, you're always finding your footing, and there was some like physicality to Ryan that that I think somewhere in there I had found, and there were some things that Carlson said about…

BRINEY: Right, there were some Jim Carrey moments, and there was like this scene that we shot at Webster Hall when I'm handing the paper through the [glass barricade], and there was just something about how cool he thinks he is, and how like flimsy he really is that really unlocked a lot of that character for me. I also think that's what makes it really sweet when you can see the moments in the movie when she starts to fall for Ryan because it's the first time she's letting herself not take her work so seriously. It's a protection, throwing yourself into work, it's like, "Oh well, I'm distracted and I don't have time for it, so that's why I'm not with somebody." I think slowly she realizes, "I can have both." There's a balance.

articles.summary: A new report tied to the sales of Grand Theft Auto 6 suggests that Rockstar's latest is already nearing 50 million copies sold. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google A new report tied to the sales of Grand Theft Auto 6 suggests that Rockstar's latest is already nearing 50 million copies sold. Not long after its launch this past week, Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, revealed that GTA 6 sold 32 million units in pre-orders alone . This led to the game making almost $4 billion on its first day and, in the process, setting a new record for an entertainment release. And while it seemed feasible that sales for GTA 6 might settle in this range for a bit, it sounds as though they only continue to skyrocket.

According to Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics, Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have already sold 44.9 million copies. Of this total, 33.7 million of the game's sales are said to have occurred on PS5, with the other 11.2 million being on Xbox platforms. Assuming that this data is accurate, it means that GTA 6 has already sold an additional 12 million copies in the four days since its arrival on November 19th.

Although Grand Theft Auto 6 has a long way to go to reach the heights seen by Grand Theft Auto 5 (which has lifetime sales of 235 million units), it's astonishing that the game is already rapidly approaching the 50 million milestone. For context, only a handful of video games in history have ever surpassed 50 million copies sold, many of which took years upon years to ever get near this threshold. GTA 6 is clearly going to catapult past this number sooner than any other game in history, and it could do so before the end of this week. At that point, it would be quickly approaching the lifetime sales of The Witcher 3 and The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim , both of which are sitting at 65 million units.

What's even more baffling about this success for Grand Theft Auto 6 is that the game has yet to even come to PC. Assuming that GTA 6 had simultaneously launched across consoles and PC, it's safe to believe that the game could have already been well past the 50 million mark. This inevitable PC release , plus the eventual launch of GTA Online in GTA 6 , will undoubtedly only continue to bring in new players, which will drive this sales total even higher. When all is said and done, GTA 6 is on pace to be one of the biggest games in history, which surely sets up Rockstar to continue pouring more resources than ever before into its next project .

How do you feel about these sales so far for Grand Theft Auto 6 ? Did you expect them to be this high, or is the game surpassing all of your expectations? Be sure to let me know for yourself down in the comments section.

articles.content:
The folks behind CBS ' Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic are hoping to make this holiday special an annual Thanksgiving week tradition.

"I feel like this is going to become part of our cultural tradition," says Scott Weintrob, founder of Studio Large Eyes and executive producer of the special. "Every Thanksgiving for the next 10 years, with the Pillsbury Bake-Off as the trigger to Thanksgiving week."

The show is actually a collaboration between CBS and General Mills — which, incidentally, owns the "Bake-Off" trademark in the United States. Balzo notes that GM, parent company of Pillsbury, had been interested in the idea of a "big grand spectacle" that would incorporate one of the company's brands. Back to that trademark: Pillsbury held its first Bake-Off in 1949, when it was called Pillsbury’s Best Grand National Baking Contest. A total of 100 finalists went to New York to compete, and each received at least $100 and kept the G.E. stove they baked on. Eleanor Roosevelt presented the grand prizes, which ranged from $25,000 to $50,000.

In the 1970s and '80s, the show hit TV and then began expanding to other cities, from Honolulu to Houston. Bob Barker hosted the broadcasts on CBS, with prizes set at $40,000 in the 1980s. Winning recipes were published in print advertisements for folks at home. (Fun fact: Peanut Blossoms, those peanut butter-flavored cookies with a Hershey's kiss in the middle, were first introduced by finalist Freda Smith in 1957, and it is one of nine recipes in the Smithsonian National Museum of American History.) In the '90s, Kurt Wait became the first $1 million grand prize, and the first male to win the title. Phylicia Rashad became the Bake-Off ’s first female host in 2000, and then the Bake-Off moved into the digital era along with a stint on Food Network.

Balzo says that baking competitions are immensely watchable because it offers inspiration for viewers at home. "The recipes they're making are so relatable, and I think people are really going to feel that when they're watching" the new show, she said, adding that many brands are trying to get into this space, and for GM, the Bake-Off special offers an "authentic connection" with Pillsbury. For 2026's Bake-Off, Weintrob began assembling a production team and then setting up meetings with distributors. With CBS on board, they set about finding a host. Having read General Mills' Wikipedia page "to the end," Weintrob learned that Drew Barrymore had appeared in a Pillsbury commercial (for its pre-made chocolate-chip cookie dough) at age 4. "I called up Pillsbury and said, 'Drew has an incredible daytime show. Drew's gotta be the host,'" Weintrob shares. "[For] the build to a show, it can't just be about the show. You've gotta get people to watch, there is amplification, there is social. This is all the responsibility of myself and my studio. With Drew, the idea was, play the commercial on your [talk] show, and announce it to the world."

Balzo agrees. She cites Barrymore's authenticity and relatability as two qualities that make her a great host. "Drew authentically remembers that experience [of the commercial], and the brand means something to her," Balzo says. "She really cares about that connection and the authenticity to the brand in this partnership, and I think people will see that come through on screen when they watch the special, which is why we're so excited to have her as our host. [In addition], we wanted this to be about more than just baking. We want to tell the stories of a diverse set of people and their backstories and what baking means to them and memories mean to them. And she's the perfect host to pull those stories out of our contestants. It was incredible to watch her on set because it felt like she was having just this intimate conversation with [the bakers]. Weintrob and showrunner Brielle Cohen watched 250 submissions from home bakers to cull the list down to 24 competitors who all have "incredible" backstories to share. In addition, famed baker and author Amirah Kassem will join Barrymore and celebrity chef judges Christina Tosi and Dook Chase in the special. It was filmed live on Oct. 23, he shares, which meant a tight turnaround for the Nov. 23 airdate.

For her part, Balzo says this was the first time General Mills had done anything "on this scale," so they really leaned on Weintrob and the production team to guide them through the process, though GM did play a hand in everything from creative direction to final casting to set direction to the judges and host. Weintrob says having a strong relationship with brands is going to be important in the future of TV and advertising. "We are not reinventing the wheel," he acknowledges. "Brands and television have always been connected. Pairing a brand with entertainment is the job of someone like myself. I see incredible opportunity because brands have very clear audiences that they want to get towards. This is what I call brand-inspired entertainment, which is there for the new consumer. It satisfies the existing consumer, but it also offers tremendous opportunity to reach a consumer that may not have heard of General Mills, Pillsbury, their cookies, their variety of product. But, he adds, it's not just matching a brand with a network and assuming the magic will happen. He says there is a lot of listening on his end and working with the brand to understand what they need while at the same time creating something that's right for a distributor and their audience. "You've got to create bespoke entertainment for a brand," he summarizes. "You can't just send them random ideas."

There's also the challenge of the promotional timeline for brands vs. distributors. Brands usually begin working on their promotional campaigns months out, while the distributors work on a shorter timeline, sometimes even just weeks. Weintrob says he worked with both companies to come up with an approach that benefited each of them.

Both Weintrob and Balzo hope this special becomes an annual tradition that families can enjoy for years. And, Weintrob suggests, the special could expand to include Valentine's Day or Super Bowl editions, for example.

"As a brand and especially the Pillsbury brand, the whole family is so important," Balzo adds. "So we wanted to make sure that we created something that could be one of those moments to bring families together around and create memories around."

articles.title: Yahya Abdul-Mateen II Addresses Marvel Future After Wonder Man Cancellation, And It Sounds Promising

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Yes, of course Yahya Abdul-Mateen II would play Wonder Man again. The actor is game if the studio is, as he made clear in a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter . Abdul-Mateen II's take on the character was one of the more unusual updates from the comics to the MCU, as it posited the cosmic superhero was, in fact, still a fictional superhero within the MCU. Simon Williams was merely an actor, but when he got the role of Wonder Man, his secret super powers came to the fore. By the end of the show's first and only season, Simon Williams was now a powered-up Wonder Man, on the run after freeing his friend Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley), who had once again impersonated the arch-criminal Mandarin, this time to cover for Simon.

A second season was announced , and then canceled . But like so many Marvel heroes on Disney+ TV shows, Simon Williams is still out there somewhere, and you'd think he'd want to lend a hand when global threats emerge. "If the phone rings, then I’m looking forward to it," he says. "I’m absolutely looking forward to it. We’ll see what happens."

If Wonder Man remains a one-and-done, Abdul-Mateen II, like Nicolas Cage with Spider-Noir , is nonetheless completely satisfied with what he got to do. "No bitterness attached to it at all," he says, when asked if there is any. "I’ve already won. I got to play Simon Williams. I had my turn to do that. People love the show, and because of the [Emmy] nomination, we were still talking about Simon." As far as the potential for more, he's clear what he thinks: "The story is alive, and Simon Williams is. I think we did something really special with that iteration of Wonder Man ." (Not that Simon dying would necessarily be any obstacle to returning in a comic-book universe.)

Yahya Abdul-Mateen II is a man seemingly born to play superheroic and iconic roles. He has the physique, and the range, and has already played two major DC characters with opposite temperaments: Dr. Manhattan in HBO's Watchmen , and Black Manta in two Aquaman movies. The former is all-knowing and aloof; the latter a volatile nutjob. There's nothing to say he couldn't play a different Marvel character, as Gemma Chan has. Indeed, Abdul-Mateen's own filmography suggests a way — he has twice previously played reboots of classic characters made famous by other indelible actors, as Morpheus in The Matrix Resurrections , and Candyman in Nia DaCosta's re-quel. When the Marvel Cinematic Universe inevitably reboots at the end of Secret Wars , he could make it a third-time charm as a new incarnation of another hero.

Simon Williams' story could also continue in a Shang-Chi sequel, given that the master of kung fu is also an ally of Trevor Slattery, and knows he's not the real Mandarin. The actual Ten Rings organization could shelter both of them as needed. Still, there's something quite dramatically ironic about the Wonder Man actor waiting by the phone for his callback, as that's absolutely something Simon Williams would do. Maybe a sequel could go meta, and be about Yahya Abdul-Mateen II the actor becoming Simon Williams the actor becoming Wonder Man the character. Whatever the case, Abdul-Mateen II is fun to watch in anything, so whether Marvel or otherwise, he'll continue to work in great projects for sure. Lucasfilm probably already has ideas, too.

Do you want more from Simon Williams' story? Or could Abdul-Mateen II play another character? Give us your best casting agent impersonation in comments.

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Crunchyroll is featuring a lot of anime currently airing this season. However, arguably the coolest fight of this year has emerged from one of Fall 2026's hottest anime, and no one expected it, precisely because the series' premise does not initially incorporate action as its main element. The anime, initially dubbed the replacement for Solo Leveling this fall, Overgeared has emerged as a series of its own, delivering some of the best crafting action and now a straight-up action sequence in its latest episode that stands on the same level as major anime such as Jujutsu Kaisen , Bleach , Black Clover , and many others. The surprising element is that it comes from the studio behind One-Punch Man Seasons 2 and 3, which has been dubbed the studio that ruined a masterpiece.

Overgeared has been standing out since the start, initially thanks to its protagonist, who stands out through his desperation. With Grid's main goal being to acquire money and his primary ability revolving around crafting, the series established itself with a different kind of protagonist and action sequences that stood out thanks to their crafting element . However, the series continued to incorporate action as well, given that combat is a core element of MMORPGs. Now, the latest episode features roughly six to seven minutes of action that matches the climactic sequences of a high-budget anime film.

Overgeared Episode 9, titled "Comrades in the Guild," continues the fight between Tzedakah's guild and Malaxus, the leader of the Yatan cult, with Grid joining the raid as well. With Grid possessing the Shield of Yatan, he boosts the confidence of the guild members, and the fight begins, featuring every member playing their role. It starts with the Macho Man delivering close-combat action that is perfectly animated, offering the kind of hand-to-hand combat that the Naruto series has often showcased. Following this, two more characters appear, fighting Malaxus with a sword and a spear. This is where one of the most beautiful shots is captured, as the camera pans across the action, delivering a captivating sequence.

Following this, the characters with projectile abilities attack Malaxus one by one, with every attack visually enhanced. This culminates in the guild's leader, Jishuka, firing a beautiful arrow. However, even that is not enough to take down Malaxus. Fortunately, Grid's mana ability has increased significantly , allowing him to display his main-character energy by unleashing his signature Pagma's Sword Dance and defeating the villain in a perfect closing sequence. Overall, this entire sequence, which lasts around six to seven minutes, is on the level of an animated movie, culminating in a battle where everyone joins forces to take down the main villain, giving their all and risking everything.

This high-quality animation is particularly surprising because this arc isn't even that major, nor is the anime nearing the conclusion of its season. However, the biggest surprise is that it comes from J.C. Staff, a studio that anime fans had given up on due to its reputation for ruining the One-Punch Man anime . It seems that with Overgeared , J.C. Staff is redeeming its reputation, raising hopes that the finale will be even more epically crafted and further establish the series as Crunchyroll's hottest Fall 2026 anime, featuring some of the coolest fights this year has to offer.

Apple TV has picked up a fifth season of the Emmy-winning comedy, which remains one of the streamer's biggest shows. Ted Lasso fans have something extra to be thankful for this Thanksgiving: the popular Apple TV comedy series has been officially renewed for a fifth season. Its targeted production start date is April 14, I hear.

The renewal, which has been pending since the Season 4 finale was released in early October, was never in doubt — four seasons in, Ted Lasso remains Apple TV's biggest global hit.

But, because Ted Lasso has been such a big juggernaut, comes from an outside studio, Warner Bros. Television, and has an executive producer and star, Jason Sudeikis , who is very protective of his creation, deals on the show have never been quick and easy. Further complicating the process this time is the fact that the Season 4 finale dropped the same day as Warner Bros. TV parent Warner Bros. Because of that, character story arcs are yet to be locked in but it's safe to assume that stars/co-creators Sudeikis (Ted Lasso) and Brendan Hunt (Coach Beard) would be back, joined by fellow OGs Hannah Waddingham (Rebecca), Jeremy Swift (Higgins), Brett Goldstein (Roy) and Juno Temple (Keeley) as well as at least some of the new Season 4 additions, most notably breakout Tanya Reynolds as Coach Alice Chilton.

The renewal comes with a question about the extent of involvement of Goldstein, who has two other series, Apple TV's Shrinking , on which he is co-creator and executive producer, and Prime Video's upcoming Escorted, which he created, executive produces and headlines, in addition to his movie career. In the Season 4 finale, Roy (Goldstein) left AFC Richmond after accepting an offer to become a manager of his former team Chelsea as he and Keeley (Temple) are expecting their first child together. The cliffhanger is an insurance policy, according to Hunt.

"No, not necessarily," he told Deadline last month when asked whether the plot twist means that Goldstein would no longer be a series regular on Ted Lasso ." It is acknowledging that he’s a busy man and giving us some wiggle room I would say. But no, there’s no expectation of losing Roy and Keeley. But they are two very busy people, so wiggle room is a smart thing."

Back after a three-year break, Ted Lasso delivered the most viewed season for a returning Apple TV comedy over the first 54 days, according to the streamer.

In the U.S., Ted Lasso set series highs for monthly viewership, drawing 3.6 billion minutes across September 1–30, and premiere week (August 3–9) with 866 million minutes.

And, despite some midway wobbles, Ted Lasso ended strong creatively, with Season 4 averaging 90% on Rotten Tomatoes.

The season expanded the Ted Lasso universe to AFC Richmond's Lady Greyhounds, introducing new characters and stories.

In it, Ted (Sudeikis) returned to Richmond, taking on his biggest challenge yet: coaching a second division women’s football team. In addition to Emmy winner Sudeikis, the fourth season also starred Emmy Award-winner Hannah Waddingham, Juno Temple, Emmy Award winner Brett Goldstein, Brendan Hunt and Jeremy Swift, along with Jude Mack, Faye Marsay, Rex Hayes, Aisling Sharkey, Abbie Hern and Grant Feely. Season four also welcomed Tanya Reynolds as Alice Chilton

The finale shook up the team's leadership, with Ted (Sudeikis) stepping back to become assistant coach alongside Coach Beard (Hunt) while promoting Alice Chilton (Reynolds) to take over as head coach from him.

"I’m certainly interested in finding out like, is this a bit pie in the sky for Ted to think he can just shift down to backseat and have someone telling him what to do and where to be and making demands of him?," Hunt said about the new dynamic. "We’ll see how how he adjusted that. It might not be as easy as he thinks."

Season 4 of Ted Lasso is executive produced by Sudeikis alongside Hunt, Joe Kelly, Jane Becker, Jamie Lee, Bill Wrubel and Jack Burditt. Goldstein serves as writer and executive producer alongside Leann Bowen. Bill Lawrence executive produces via his Doozer Productions, in association with Warner Bros. Television and Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group. Doozer’s Jeff Ingold and Liza Katzer also serve as executive producers. The series was developed by Sudeikis, Lawrence, Kelly and Hunt, and is based on the preexisting format and characters from NBC Sports.

The first season became the most Emmy Award-nominated comedy series, and the series went on to land rare back-to-back Emmys for Outstanding Comedy Series for its first two seasons on air.

articles.summary: John Turturro may have earned some of his biggest paychecks from Michael Bay's "Transformers" franchise, but the actor says there's a danger in doing too many Hollywood blockbusters. articles.content:
John Turturro may have earned some of his biggest paychecks from Michael Bay's "Transformers" franchise, but the actor says there's a danger in doing too many Hollywood blockbusters.

Speaking at the Marrakech International Film Festival about his decision to join the blockbuster franchise, Turturro recalled advice he received from Robert Redford, who directed him in the 1994 film "Quiz Show." Related Stories NBCUniversal, Hornbill Capital Back EloElo, Parent of Indian Microdrama Platform Story TV, in $80 Million Funding Round India's T-Series and Hungama Launch Microdrama Platform FastTV With $32 Million Commitment (EXCLUSIVE)

"He said, 'It's good to work both sides of the street,'" Turturro said, referring to lucrative studio projects versus more personal, creative pursuits. "You can cross the street, and you can always go back as long as you don't do too much of it in a row." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Turturro explained that spending too much time on commercial projects can come at the expense of an actor's creative instincts. "What happens is you can lose your inner life," he said. "You want to feed your inner life. That's like your fireplace. You want to feed that."

The actor, who played the eccentric Agent Seymour Simmons in four "Transformers" films between 2007 and 2017, said the franchise required a different creative approach than his independent work. "It's not like a fine painting. It's more like when Picasso does the quick sketch type of thing, and you've got to kind of do it like you're playing with your kids," Turturro said. "There's a challenge to that. Can you do that or not?"

He added that "Michael Bay liked working with me because I basically play a version of him in some ways."

The actor also acknowledged — not for the first time — the financial benefits of taking on a major Hollywood franchise. "They pay me a lot more money, so then I can do all these other projects," he said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Turturro recalled how his children encouraged him to take the "Transformers" role after years of turning down big-budget studio offers. In one instance, he passed on a substantial paycheck for the 1999 superhero comedy "Mystery Men" after his daughter read the script and gave him a less-than-enthusiastic review.

"They offered me a ton of money. I've never made this much money," Turturro said but when he showed his daughter the script she called it "garbage."

At the time, Turturro was also considering a stage production of Samuel Beckett's "Waiting for Godot." After reading the first eight pages of the play together, his daughter had a very different reaction: "This is good. This is very good." Turturro ultimately chose the play, where he earned just $300 a week.

Turtorro concluded with a final analogy: "I consider myself a plumber in my real work, and [commercial movies] are sort of my electrical job."

Turturro's latest project, "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York," also screened at Marrakech following his Golden Star tribute on Sunday night . Directed by Noah Segan and produced by Rian Johnson and Ram Bergman's T-Street, the indie crime drama stars Turturro as an aging pickpocket struggling to make ends meet in a rapidly changing New York City. The film, which also stars Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito and Tatiana Maslany, premiered at Sundance earlier this year and was acquired by Sony Pictures Classics.

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The Half-Life remake just got a major update. When the original Half-Life came out in 1998, it revolutionized the first-person shooter genre. Then in 2004, Valve did it again with Half-Life 2 . Unfortunately, while the Half-Life 3 rumors persist , right now the series remains on ice, much like the rest of Valve's back catalog. In 2020, fans took it upon themselves to release a remake/reimagining of the first game titled Black Mesa . And Valve not only allowed it, but also allowed it to be released on Steam, where it proved to be very popular. To this end, it has nearly 71,000 user reviews on Steam to date, with a 94% approval rating.

Right now, it's on sale for $5, down from $20, but more noteworthy than that, it just got a major update, and this major update added Steam Deck verification. Previously, it was playable on the Steam Deck, but now it is Steam Deck Verified. This means Valve has confirmed the PC game works from start to finish and works well with the built-in display and controls of the Steam Deck. At least this is what it's supposed to mean. Practically, it doesn't always quite mean this because the standard of verification is perhaps not as strict as it should be.

Not only did the game get Steam Deck verified, but it got a major update as well. To this end, there are visual upgrades, engine optimizations, and a complete interface overhaul. The update also notably and substantially improves mod support.

BAFTA is losing the longtime headline sponsor of its film awards, EE.

The Brit mobile and internet provider has sponsored the UK's leading film awards event for almost 30 years but the upcoming 2027 edition will be its last.

The decision was driven by EE’s “business strategy,” according to BAFTA, which said it was first told about the move at the end of 2025. The news was first reported in UK trade publication Campaign.
